item.title: With El-Sayed’s Victory Comes a Wave of Islamophobia
item.description:
Senator Tommy Tuberville called Dr. Abdul El-Sayed a “terrorist.”

Representative Nancy Mace described “every single Muslim holding public office in America” as “a threat to both national security and our republic.”

And on Monday, President Trump said that there were “jihadists being elected all over the place.”

In the days since Dr. El-Sayed’s victory in Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary, Republican leaders have embraced Islamophobic attacks and falsehoods like those three comments to portray him as an anti-American extremist. The onslaught is being fueled in part by Republican Party officials and has quickly become a central aspect of the strategy to beat Dr. El-Sayed in the fall. Few officials in the Republican Party have publicly tried to tamp down such messaging, though Dr. El-Sayed has not hesitated to parry the attacks.

“They’re going to point at me, they’re going to point at my name, like, ‘Wow, he’s different,’” he said the morning after his win. “My name is not raising your gas prices,” he added. “My name is not taking us to war. My name is not the reason you can’t afford your groceries.”

Muslim and Arab American political power is growing across the country, led by prominent figures including Zohran Mamdani, the mayor of New York City, and Dr. El-Sayed, who is the son of Egyptian immigrants and was born in Michigan. The number of Muslim American running for — and winning — local, state and federal elections has steadily increased over the past decade. Today, there are more than 230 elected Muslim officials, according to the Council on American-Islamic Relations, including four Muslim Americans in Congress, the highest number ever.

Three more could be elected to the House this fall. And in Michigan last week, several Arab Americans won contested primaries, including for the state legislature and mayor of Ann Arbor.

But the increase in power has also drawn considerable repercussions. Muslim officials say that their increased visibility has brought with it a wave of bigotry and threats. In recent years, Mr. Trump has repeatedly attacked Representative Ilhan Omar, an immigrant, mocking her hijab and declaring that she should be “sent back” to Somalia. Multiple Republicans have falsely accused Mr. Mamdani of being a jihadist.

“There has been remarkable political progress for Muslims in American, but the backlash to that has come in the form of anti-Muslim hate that seems to be the worst we have seen yet,” said Edward Ahmed Mitchell, the national deputy director for CAIR, one of the largest Muslim advocacy groups in the United States. Mr. Mitchell said that much of the negative response has stemmed from candidates’ criticism of Israel over the past several years.

“We have a generation who became very forceful at speaking for themselves,” Mr. Mitchell said. “They essentially said we are not going to take this anymore, we are not going to be begging for scraps.”

Many of these new leaders have made Palestinian rights and an end to military aid to Israel central to their platforms, arguing that such assistance directly undercuts spending on U.S. health care, housing and public schools. Their wins have helped shift the politics within the Democratic Party, where support for Israel now amounts to a liability in some quarters.

That change has helped fuel Republicans claims that the party is electing extremist candidates. Mike Pompeo, the former secretary of state, accused Dr. El-Sayed of being a “Hamas supporter.” Dr. El-Sayed has condemned the group.

The attacks have not been limited to Muslim and Arab American politicians’ views on Israel. More broadly, they have tried to depict candidates as out of step with the country, sometimes dangerously so.

The first advertisement against Dr. El-Sayed from the National Republican Senatorial Committee last week called him “the most radical Senate candidate in America” and pointedly referred to him by his full name, Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed.

Mike Rogers, the Republican Senate candidate in Michigan, accused Dr. El Sayed of believing that the United States “deserved” the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks — a sentiment he has denied. Hasan Piker, the left-wing podcaster Dr. El-Sayed has campaigned with, voiced that view but later called it “inappropriate.”

Days later, Mr. Trump juxtaposed two photographs in a social media post, one of himself standing next to Melania Trump in a strapless dress, and the other of Dr. El-Sayed sitting next to his wife, who was wearing a hijab. “Two VERY DIFFERENT America’s,” the president wrote.

Last week, Senator Ted Cruz, Republican of Texas, held a hearing on what he called the threat of the Muslim Brotherhood network in America, after saying that Dr. El-Sayed and other Democrats “hate America.”

In a House primary in Michigan last week, a little-known Republican who had suspended his own campaign beat Amir Hassan, a Navy veteran who had Mr. Trump’s endorsement and is Christian. A third candidate in the race acknowledged that his campaign created advertisements that “didn’t so much appeal to bigotry against Muslims as kind of counted on it.”

Asked about such tactics in a television interview over the weekend, Senator Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, who recently lost a bid for re-election, said he condemned the bigoted comments from his fellow Republicans. “Everybody should be treated as an individual,” he said. But few other high-profile Republicans have spoken out against such language.

It’s not clear what impact such speech has with voters. Representative Andy Ogles of Tennessee, who has made statements like “Muslims don’t belong in American society,” lost his Republican primary last week.

On Sunday, Dr. El-Sayed pushed back against Mr. Trump’s notion of two Americas by attacking the president’s marriage while praising his own.

“Yes, you’ve got two different visions of America,” he said in an interview on CNN. “One in which your overlords are two people who don’t like each other but joined in the interest of making billions of dollars off of you, or two people who genuinely love each other, enjoyed some pancakes together, want to come together to build the kind of America where they can raise a family, and know that that family is going to have the good things.”

CAIR estimates that there are more than 2.5 million Muslims registered to vote across the country, with many concentrated in key battleground states.

Nowhere is the rise to power among Muslim political leaders and activists more consequential than in Michigan, a swing state with the highest concentration of Arab Americans in the country. In 2020, President Joseph R. Biden Jr. carried the state with overwhelming support from Dearborn, a city where Arab Americans make up a majority of the population. But in 2024, as the Biden administration continued to support Israel during its bombardment in Gaza, many of those voters were disillusioned. Mr. Trump won Dearborn by six percentage points and helped to flip Michigan, as Democratic turnout in Muslim-majority precincts plummeted.

“As Arab Americans, we have more power than we’ve ever had,” said Abbas Alawieh, a former congressional staffer and longtime Democratic organizer. Last week, Mr. Alawieh easily won a Democratic primary in a newly drawn State Senate district that includes the highest concentration of Muslim and Arab American voters in Michigan.

In 2024, Mr. Alawieh helped create the “Uncommitted” campaign, encouraging Democratic voters not to cast a ballot for Mr. Biden to show their opposition to the war in Gaza. He called Dr. El-Sayed’s primary victory a “monumental shift in our politics.”

“We are reaching disillusioned voters and changing the conception of what is possible,” he said.

In the days leading up to Michigan’s primary election, organizers from Emgage, which focuses on empowering Muslim voters, knocked on more than 15,000 doors and sent nearly a million text messages targeting registered voters. Organizers from the Council on American-Islamic Relations called more than 48,000 Michigan voters to encourage them to cast their ballots.

Dr. El-Sayed performed strongly in significant Arab American populations. In Dearborn, he won nearly 80 percent of the vote and 70 percent of the vote in nearby Dearborn Heights.

Yet for all of the history-making potential of his campaign, Dr. El-Sayed and his supporters often hesitate to frame his platform around identity. In an interview last week with The New York Times, he resisted a question about the potential of becoming the country’s first Muslim senator.

“I think this is a moment for people who want to bring integrity back to our politics,” he said. “I’m just interested in being the next U.S. senator from Michigan. Yes, I have an uncommon name, which they’re going to point to a lot. But I know America is big enough for people with names like mine. People are asking less about how you pray than what you pray for.”

And he has repeatedly emphasized his optimism.

“This is the best place in the world to be Abdul,” he said the morning after his win.

Tim Balk contributed reporting.

item.title: How Iran Adapted Its Attacks as U.S. War Munitions Dwindled
item.description:
During five intense days last month, Iran launched waves of drones and missiles at U.S. troops on three bases in Jordan, hoping to break through the formidable American air defenses.

Using advanced missiles that can suddenly change course, Iran pummeled the bases’ defensive systems, forcing the Americans to burn through scarce supplies of Patriot interceptors.

On the fifth day, the Iranians broke through.

A missile struck prefabricated housing units at one of the bases on July 17, killing three U.S. soldiers and wounding more than 100. Pentagon officials later acknowledged that scores of other troops were injured and several aircraft damaged in attacks in Jordan that week.

“We shot down almost all the missiles,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio said when asked about the fatal attack. “One leaked through.”

The strikes reveal a deadly confluence of two important trends: First, Iran has become a more skilled adversary as the war has progressed, learning how to evade U.S. air defenses as it widened the battlefield to include most of the Middle East and enlisted allies like the Houthis in Yemen and militias in Iraq.

Second, the Pentagon’s supply of interceptors has quickly dwindled, with the weapons becoming more precious each day of the off-and-on conflict.

The two trends drive home a point that has slowly emerged in the months since the war started, that a global superpower with a mighty military footprint can still be held at bay by a lesser adversary willing to wage asymmetric warfare to find any advantage it can.

The Pentagon has used more than 1,500 Patriot interceptor missiles in the war and has fewer than 1,700 interceptors left, according to two people briefed on the stockpile levels who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military details. The United States produced about 600 interceptors in all of 2025.

The rapid depletion is occurring as Iranian forces study another war. In Ukraine, Russia has used combinations of ballistic and cruise missiles to distract Ukrainian air defenses, and then rushed in drones.

“The Iranians are making it more difficult on air defenses when you have a range of both missiles and drones coming in,” said Seth G. Jones, the president of the defense and security department at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

“They have effectively leveraged the Russian tactic,” he said, “to make it more difficult to protect across locations in the Gulf.”

On a single day during that deadly week last month, according to two U.S. officials, American forces in the Middle East fired about 50 Patriot interceptors, which cost about $4 million each.

The Pentagon has continued to face a powerful threat, which it has tried to minimize, in the months since major combat ended in early April.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told reporters on April 8 that Iran’s missile program was “functionally destroyed,” that its launchers and missiles were “depleted and decimated and almost completely ineffective.”

Most of Iran’s missiles and launchers were stored in vast underground facilities that U.S. and Israeli forces heavily bombed during the first five weeks of the war. But Iran dug out many of those sites and resumed firing, bringing shipping in the Strait of Hormuz to a near standstill and threatening American troops in the region.

President Trump and his national security advisers assumed the fight would be short and would not jeopardize the Pentagon’s stockpiles of Patriot interceptors, said Vali Nasr, a professor at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies.

But Tehran, he and other Iran experts say, had been waiting for this moment since the conflict began more than five months ago. During a 12-day war in June 2025, Iran’s leaders had seen how quickly Israeli and American forces burned through ballistic missile interceptors to knock down barrages of Iranian drones and missiles.

Iran’s deadliest strikes against U.S. forces in Jordan targeted Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Azraq, a Jordanian military installation that the U.S. Air Force has increasingly used as a major hub for dozens of aircraft and several thousand service members.

Many U.S. troops previously stationed in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates were moved before and during the war to bases like Muwaffaq Salti in Jordan that were farther from Iran and deemed safer from drone and ballistic attacks.

In the days immediately after the strike on July 17, American military commanders strengthened air defenses in Jordan and elsewhere in the region, said a senior U.S. military official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss operational matters but declined to provide more details.

U.S. military specialists who have also studied drone and missile attacks in Ukraine have been working with the military’s Central Command for months, sharing lessons learned from that campaign. Two of the three soldiers killed in Jordan were assigned to air defense units based in Germany that became part of that effort.

This new reality is having geopolitical consequences.

In late July, Mr. Trump asked Mr. Hegseth about the dwindling American weapons supplies, U.S. officials said, confirming reporting by The Washington Post.

The Pentagon has maintained publicly that it does not have a shortfall. “Claims of U.S. munition shortages are false,” the chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement. “When the fake news media irresponsibly amplifies these lies, the real-world consequence is clear: Our enemies are emboldened to provoke — or attack — American troops.”

Two weeks ago, Mr. Trump called off bombing raids against Iran after he said the leaders of Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar had asked him to pursue diplomatic talks to end the war, which has killed an estimated 1,700 Iranian civilians.

In a phone call, Mohammed bin Salman, the de facto ruler of Saudi Arabia, told Mr. Trump that major airstrikes would probably prompt Iran to retaliate against energy sites and other infrastructure in the kingdom and its neighbors, according to a Saudi official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss confidential discussions.

With the United States running low on interceptors and Iran’s demonstrating that it could pierce those defenses, the threat of serious damage was very real, the Saudi official said. Prince Mohammed urged Mr. Trump to de-escalate, the official said.

The Jordan attack was not the first time Iran has adapted its skills and tactics in this war.

In April, Iran shot down an American F-15E fighter jet over southern Iran with a shoulder-fired surface-to-air missile. Both the pilot and the weapons officer ejected. The pilot was rescued quickly, but the weapons officer was missing for nearly two days, hiding from Iranian security forces until U.S. Special Operations forces rescued him in a daring operation.

In this case, Iran learned from Ukraine and deployed a swarm of drones in an area American fighter jets had penetrated, a senior U.S. military official said. In interviews with Pentagon officials, the crew said that the F-15E’s defensive countermeasures provided only half a second of warning before Iran hit the $60 million advanced fighter jet with a shoulder-fired missile.

American military officials concluded that the drones fed three critical pieces of information to Iranian commanders that helped them target the F-15E: its GPS location, speed and direction, one senior military official said.

Mr. Trump announced a “pause” in the fighting shortly after that incident. Military officials needed time to adjust to Iran’s new tactics, two military officials said.

Even during breaks in fighting, those tactics have continued to evolve.

When the Houthi militia in Yemen entered the war last month, experts said it signaled Iran’s intention to force the United States and its allies to defend themselves from aerial attacks from all directions. Yemen is hundreds of miles south of Iran.

International inspectors also believe that Iran is storing elements of its nuclear program in a heavily fortified underground complex in central Iran. The site, which the United States refers to as Pickaxe Mountain, is buried more than 300 feet beneath a mountain.

And Iran has sent its troops and leaders to hide-outs scattered across the country, experts said.

“Where are they?” asked Mr. Nasr, of Johns Hopkins. “It’s not like they’re sitting in a place where you can bomb them. You don’t find them.”

Jonathan Swan contributed reporting.

item.title: Ocasio-Cortez Opened Up About Freezing Her Eggs. She Got Women Talking.
item.description:
Eight long years ago, Meg Quinn decided not to share the details of a big decision.

She was 37 and just out of a long-term relationship when she started panicking. Was she running out of time to have children? Feeling helpless, she decided to do something that was expensive but might help her chances of becoming a mother.

She froze her eggs.

“It was hard to talk about,” Ms. Quinn, a food content creator who’s now 45, said on Monday in an interview from her home in Los Angeles. “There were so many different ways that it could go. Like, you could spend all this money and it could be for nothing.”

So when Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, 36, announced last weekend that she would be freezing her eggs — and then posted video on Instagram injecting herself with medication just before a TV interview — Ms. Quinn was stunned by the boldness of her actions.

“I just love that she’s making it public,” she said. “I think women, the more we share, the better it is.”

She added: “It’s hard on women. We have to do all these things, and, like, no guy has to do these things.”

Until about 2012, freezing eggs to preserve fertility was considered an experimental intervention for urgent cases like cancer patients whose fertility would be compromised by treatment.

But it’s only now, as thousands more go through a process, that women are freely talking about it.

Like breast cancer, menopause and menstruation, egg freezing has become yet another women’s health issue in which open discussion is seen as a form of empowerment. Ms. Ocasio-Cortez herself said that it was “badass that I’m going to be giving myself shots in the green room” of a TV studio.

Her very personal disclosure, however, also had a political overtones, as she linked her decision to freeze her eggs to the debates over reproductive choice.

“There is very strangely a political risk, or a political tax, that comes with sharing this info,” she said, adding that she wanted “to show more depictions of women having full lives in every context and every choice.”

Indeed, her announcement also brought disquiet over the medical messaging and outright condemnation of her choices.

Though some people refer to freezing eggs as an insurance policy, doctors said that it was not always a smooth process and hardly guaranteed fertility later in life. Conservative commentators, especially those who have decried the country’s dropping birthrate, said that in vitro fertilization and other reproductive technologies give women the false impression that they can wait to have children.

Allie Beth Stuckey, the popular conservative writer and commentator, posted: “She’s glamorizing the lie that women can have it all. You can’t. Biology is real and how you order your life makes or breaks your future.”

Whatever the risks or the politics, the rate of egg freezing has soared: In the decade between 2014 and 2024, the number of egg freezing cycles grew to 38,930 from 6,090, according to Dr. Jennifer Eaton, president of the Society for Assisted Reproductive Technology.

Many women see egg freezing as a reflection of the times, as they search for ways to navigate their education, careers and relationships. In interviews, they described a personal decision, which could be both empowering, but also defensive, in case their hopes of finding suitable life partners do not materialize.

Egg freezing seems natural, said Karina Martin, who is 34 and lives in Sacramento. She underwent the procedure two years ago, before studying to be a physician assistant. She said she initially thought she would be ready to use the eggs in about five years. If she has to have a baby alone, she said, she will do it.

She sympathizes with Ms. Ocasio-Cortez’s decision to preserve her options. “She is a hard-working woman who has put her career first,” she said. “It’s a really smart decision, and I don’t think it’s political.”

Avni Barman, the chief executive of the media company Gen She, froze her eggs last year, even though she was in a serious relationship and didn’t expect to need them.

Ms. Barman, 29, posted videos of the process, hoping to show that it is not difficult, especially for younger women. “I feel so powerful,” she said, because she was taking control of something she didn’t want to leave up to chance.

On her videos, she explained that the cost to freeze her eggs in New York City was about $7,000 and that she easily squeezed the procedure into her busy day, which included a conference and an investor dinner.

“I’m friends with a lot of really successful seven, eight, nine-figure female founders — they all do it,” Ms. Barman said in an interview. “To them, it’s like getting a designer bag — freezing your eggs, they cost the same — and that’s kind of the mentality around it.”

Doctors and experts, however, say the process is often not that easy. Egg freezing and other fertility treatments can be as stressful as cancer treatments, said Rena Gower, a fertility therapist based in Manhattan.

A woman must inject a cocktail of hormonal medications into her abdomen over a period of eight to 12 days. A doctor then retrieves the eggs by a needle inserted through the vaginal wall while the patient is sedated.

Mature eggs are flash frozen in liquid nitrogen, potentially preserving them for many years. It is essentially the first step of in vitro fertilization, which involves thawing the eggs, fertilizing them in the lab and creating embryos.

Many infertility doctors said they hope that Ms. Ocasio-Cortez’s transparency will lead to a bigger, clearer conversation about supporting a woman’s desire to have children.

Right now, fertility is poorly understood, they said.

“I’ve had patients come in at age 48, and I’m ready to start talking about menopause, and they’re ready to start talking about fertility,” said Dr. Audrey Buxbaum, a gynecologist at Downtown Women in Manhattan.

Ms. Gower, the fertility therapist, said that she has encountered many women who were afraid to tell anyone that they have frozen their eggs.

Sometimes, she said, women feel forced into secrecy by their families, who believe it is morally wrong. Or they feel guilt or shame that their body might be seen as broken, or that their romantic relationships aren’t working out.

Some women are nervous that motherhood — even the prospect of it — would negatively influence their jobs.

Ms. Quinn, the content creator who was surprised by Ms. Ocasio-Cortez’s openness, said freezing her eggs left her so drained that she felt numb.

She dove into her savings to pay about $16,000 for the initial cycle, which produced only seven of the 18 frozen eggs her doctor had hoped for.

She was devastated. The doctor suggested she complete one or two more cycles, but she couldn’t bear even the idea of it, emotionally or financially.

Two years later, in 2020, she met her life partner, Greg Gomes. And on Feb. 14, 2023, when Ms. Quinn was 42, a doctor implanted the embryo that became their daughter, Rory.

On Valentine’s Day of this year, Ms. Quinn felt brave enough to post the details of her motherhood journey on social media, and the lessons she learned. She wanted to give people hope “because there’s so much unknown before you get to this place.”

The title was, “I froze my eggs at 37.”

“I feel more confident to talk about it,” she said, “now that it has worked out.”

Annie Karni contributed reporting. Alain Delaquérière and Kirsten Noyes contributed research.

item.title: In Minnesota, a Moderate Democrat Has a Big Cash Edge Over Her Liberal Rival
item.description:
Over and over this year, moderate Democrats have had big financial advantages over their progressive rivals in primary races. Over and over, the progressives have won.

Representative Angie Craig is hoping the outcome is different on Tuesday in Minnesota.

Ms. Craig, a centrist running for Senate, has a significant edge on advertising spending over her left-wing Democratic primary opponent, Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan. Ms. Craig has outspent her by more than four to one, $19.9 million versus $4.7 million, including money from allied outside groups, according to data from media tracking firm AdImpact.

Ms. Craig has been bolstered in particular by about $10 million in ad spending since late May from a low-profile group called North Star Dawn PAC.

That group — like an increasing number of super PACs with murky origins — has been funded almost entirely by a so-called dark-money nonprofit group, which allows the super PAC to avoid ever disclosing the true provenance of the cash. That nonprofit group, the Civic Progress Fund Inc., was incorporated last December in Delaware. It has also aired pro-Craig ads.

Ms. Flanagan has also sought to use Ms. Craig’s past support from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee — a major pro-Israel lobbying group that has proved highly divisive in Democratic primaries this cycle — against her. AIPAC has not endorsed Ms. Craig or directly spent money on her behalf in this race.

Ms. Flanagan has attacked Ms. Craig as the candidate of dark money. But the lieutenant governor has had her own outside spending, primarily from a group affiliated with Democratic lieutenant governors that she once led. Some of its money comes from groups with undisclosed donors.

Ads from both the lieutenant governors group and North Star Dawn have sought to portray the opposing candidate as in the pocket of special interests.

Ms. Craig’s campaign raised more money than Ms. Flanagan’s by a margin of about two to one over the course of the race, allowing the congresswoman to outspend the lieutenant governor.

item.title: When to Expect Results in Wisconsin, Minnesota, South Carolina and Beyond
item.description:
Six states — Alabama, Connecticut, Minnesota, South Carolina, Vermont and Wisconsin — are holding primaries on Tuesday. The first polls will close at 7 p.m. Eastern time.

Here’s when to expect both unofficial and certified results.

Alabama is holding special congressional primaries on Tuesday in four newly drawn districts after the state adopted new congressional maps. Polls close at 7 p.m. local time (8 p.m. Eastern), after which the election board will begin tabulating.

Early votes will be counted first, but since Alabama has a relatively rigid early voting policy, it’s likely there will be fewer of them than in other states. Ballots cast on Election Day will be next.

You can refer to The Times’s vote tracker to watch the results come in.

Connecticut’s municipalities will begin reporting their results once polls close, at 8 p.m. Eastern. Election officials say it’s likely that results will be known late on Tuesday.

The Times will be tracking results here.

Results won’t be official until Aug. 18, the state’s final deadline to certify the vote.

Polls in Minnesota close at 8 p.m. local time (9 p.m. Eastern), at which point election officials will begin tabulating. They anticipate unofficial results will be in by late Tuesday night or early Wednesday morning.

You can visit The Times’s results tracker here once polls close.

The state canvassing board will meet on Aug. 18 to certify the vote.

South Carolina has just one race on its special election ballot — the U.S. Senate seat left vacant after the death last month of Lindsey Graham.

Results will most likely come in soon after polls close at 7 p.m. Eastern time, officials expect. If no candidates gather enough votes to win the nomination outright, which is likely, the race will go to a runoff between the top two candidates, to be held Aug. 25.

The Times’s tracker will have the results as they arrive.

Vermont’s election system is decentralized, meaning that clerks representing Vermont’s 247 cities and towns are responsible for administering elections in their own districts. Most of these municipalities use voting tabulators, which makes counting ballots quicker; election officials expect all clerks to report their unofficial results by Tuesday night.

You can follow along with The Times’s election night vote tracker here once polls close, at 7 p.m. Eastern.

These results will remain unofficial until the statewide canvass occurs to certify the vote, on Aug. 18. Voters can watch the canvass on a livestream provided by the state.

Wisconsin doesn’t have a statewide system for reporting unofficial results; that is the responsibility of the state’s 72 county clerks, who will post results online as votes are counted in their respective areas.

Polls close at 8 p.m. local time (9 p.m. Eastern). Election officials warn that some cities will take longer than others to report their results — particularly large cities that must process many absentee ballots, such as Milwaukee, Green Bay, Racine and Kenosha. Results in those communities may not arrive until early on Wednesday, or even later.

You can follow along with The Times’s vote tracker here.

The results of the election will be certified by Aug. 26.

item.title: 5 Things to Know About South Carolina Senate Candidate Mark Sanford
item.description:
Mark Sanford, a former governor and congressman of South Carolina whose political career was damaged by a high-profile affair, is facing four other candidates in a special Republican Senate primary election to succeed Senator Lindsey Graham, who died last month.

Here are five things to know about Mr. Sanford.

1. He is no stranger to setbacks or comebacks. Mr. Sanford, 66, was considered a possible candidate for president in 2012 until he vanished without explanation in 2009, famously leaving his staff to tell reporters that he was hiking the Appalachian Trail. In fact, he was in the midst of an extramarital affair with a woman in Argentina. Four years later, he was elected to Congress. Since then, he launched a bid for president and filed to run for his old House seat, but he abandoned both efforts before votes were cast.

2. President Trump is not a fan. A staunch fiscal conservative, Mr. Sanford repeatedly broke with Mr. Trump on government spending, among other issues, during his last stint in Congress. As a result, Mr. Trump backed his primary election opponent in 2018, which led to Mr. Sanford’s ouster. A year later, Mr. Sanford briefly challenged Mr. Trump for the Republican presidential nomination.

3. He is pitching himself as a businessman focused on the national debt — including by giving a news conference with a pair of pigs he called “Debt” and “Deficit.” In past elections, Mr. Sanford has acknowledged that South Carolina Republicans were not in the mood for a candidate focused on fiscal conservatism. He is betting this time will be different.

4. He is widely known in South Carolina. Name recognition is an important factor in a primary election that lasted only about a month, and most people in the state know Mr. Sanford. In addition to his time as a governor, congressman and many stints as a candidate, he has prioritized private conversations with constituents and readily handed out his phone number.

5. He’s been driving around the state in a pickup on a barnstorming tour he has called the “Mama I Can’t Afford a New Truck Tour.” The tour has focused on the rising cost of everyday life.

item.title: 5 Things to Know About South Carolina Senate Candidate Ralph Norman
item.description:
Representative Ralph Norman, a longtime lawmaker aligned with the hard-line conservative wing of his party, faces four other candidates in a special Republican Senate primary election to succeed Lindsey Graham, who died last month.

Here are five things to know about Mr. Norman, 73, a five-term congressman from the South Carolina suburbs of Charlotte, N.C.

1. He lost a race for governor this year. Mr. Norman came in third place in the Republican primary in June, behind Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette and Alan Wilson, the state’s attorney general. (Mr. Wilson later defeated Ms. Evette in a runoff.) Running for governor gave Mr. Norman statewide name recognition and made it easier to run a compressed campaign for the Senate, after Mr. Graham’s death, since he had already spent plenty of time campaigning across the state. He did well in the governor’s race in several upstate counties, including Greenville County, which is rich in Republican voters.

2. He endorsed Nikki Haley for president in 2024. Mr. Norman backed Ms. Haley, the former South Carolina governor, over President Trump in the Republican presidential primary. Mr. Norman has described Ms. Haley as a friend and said he told Mr. Trump in advance about his plan to endorse one of his opponents. But supporting Ms. Haley may have cost Mr. Norman an endorsement from Mr. Trump in the governor’s race and again in the special Senate primary.

3. He is the vice chairman of the House Freedom Caucus. Mr. Norman is perhaps best known for being a member of the ultraconservative group of House members that has opposed spending bills and staunchly supported Mr. Trump’s immigration crackdown.

4. He has promised to be “very vocal” in the Senate. Mr. Norman, like his rivals, has campaigned for the Senate in part on supporting the SAVE America Act, a voting restrictions bill that Mr. Trump has made a priority of his domestic agenda. Mr. Norman has described the Senate as “deadlocked” and said getting legislation to move in the chamber again will require more stalwart conservatives to vote as they do in the House.

5. He has been a real estate developer for four decades. Mr. Norman joined his father’s construction business out of college and helped grow it into a large commercial real estate operation.

item.title: 5 Things to Know About South Carolina Senate Candidate Russell Fry
item.description:
Representative Russell Fry, a loyal Trump ally, faces four other candidates in a special Republican Senate primary election to succeed Lindsey Graham, who died last month.

Here are five things to know about Mr. Fry, 41, a two-term congressman from northeastern South Carolina.

1. He defeated a Republican who voted to impeach President Trump. In 2022, Mr. Fry ousted former Representative Tom Rice, one of the 10 House Republicans who voted to impeach Mr. Trump in 2021. That victory made Mr. Trump fond of Mr. Fry.

2. The president initially signaled he might support him in the Senate race. Two days after Mr. Graham died, Mr. Trump told Newsmax that Mr. Fry was “outstanding” and suggested that the congressman might be a contender in the Senate contest. “I could see that happening,” Mr. Trump said. “I think he’s a very, very talented person.” Mr. Trump later decided to back Darline Graham, Mr. Graham’s younger sister, who had agreed to serve out the remainder of her brother’s term.

3. He is running for Senate while also running for re-election to the House. South Carolina law allows Mr. Fry to continue his House re-election campaign while also running for Senate. But he would not be allowed to hold both offices simultaneously, so if he were to win both races, his House seat would become vacant in January. His rivals have criticized Mr. Fry for risking leaving Republicans a member short, especially if they hold on to their narrow House majority. Mr. Fry has acknowledged that the situation is “odd” but noted that his seat would remain safely Republican.

4. He has campaigned in part on his youth. If elected, Mr. Fry would become one of the youngest members of the Senate, where the median age is nearly 67 years old. “The Senate is an older body, and I think that’s what people want — they want fresh energy in there,” he said at a candidate event last week. “The old way of doing things, that’s why people are ticked.” Mr. Fry, a lawyer, has also said that his family came from modest means, so he understands voters struggling with affordability.

5. He once interned in Mr. Graham’s office. Mr. Graham’s roots in South Carolina’s Republican politics ran deep, and Mr. Fry was involved in party politics at a young age. He was later elected to the state’s General Assembly, where he served for seven years.

item.title: 5 Things to Know About South Carolina Senate Candidate Darline Graham
item.description:
Darline Graham, a longtime advocate for disability rights, is competing against four other candidates in a special Republican Senate primary election to succeed her brother, Senator Lindsey Graham, who died last month.

Except for occasional appearances alongside her brother, Ms. Graham, 62, had lived a quiet life with her family in the suburbs of Columbia, S.C., until she decided to run for the Senate. Here are five things to know about her.

1. President Trump endorsed Ms. Graham after a high-stakes meeting in the Oval Office, surprising many in South Carolina who assumed he would endorse Russell Fry, a two-term congressman and loyal ally. item.title: With Trump Secretly Evacuated, Imperiled Air Force One Became a Flying Decoy
item.description:
The threat to Air Force One was seen as so dire that they sneaked President Trump off the jet in a catering container to keep him safe. But the same dire threat did not stop them from then sending Air Force One into the skies anyway with a planeful of government employees, reporters and military personnel serving as decoys.

If the Iranians really were trying to shoot down the presidential plane last month, as U.S. officials concluded at the time, then the subterfuge in Ankara, Turkey, that protected the president also may have made targets of dozens of other people who flew aboard the jet, some of them unaware that Mr. Trump was not actually with them because it was considered too dangerous.

The government has on rare occasions engaged in sleight of hand to safeguard presidents from possible jeopardy, particularly for journeys to hazardous locations, such as when George W. Bush or Barack Obama flew to Iraq during days of war or when Bill Clinton made a brief visit to Pakistan with its history of terrorism. The Trump team’s ruse in Ankara, however, stands out not only for its misdirection but also for the way it shifted the evident peril to others and was kept secret long after Mr. Trump was out of harm’s way.

“They just didn’t seem to give a second thought to anybody but the president and the few people who were with him,” said Joe Lockhart, who served as White House press secretary to Mr. Clinton during his 2000 trip to Islamabad, the Pakistani capital. “We went out of our way to make sure the maximum number of people, especially civilians, were protected and not human shields. They didn’t even think about it. And to me, that’s the big difference.”

But other veterans of risky White House trips said there were times that extreme measures were justified to protect the president. Joseph W. Hagin, who as a top adviser to Mr. Bush helped organize his war zone trips and later served as Mr. Trump’s deputy White House chief of staff in his first term, said he would not second-guess the decision in Ankara.

“I understand there is concern for those flying on what was assumed to be the primary aircraft,” Mr. Hagin said, “but when you go to work at the White House or travel with the president, you are accepting a not-insignificant degree of risk. Telling everyone what’s up in an operation like this would have obviously jeopardized the president’s safety.”

When Mr. Bush or Mr. Obama brought staff members and reporters with them to war zones, Mr. Hagin added, those were dangerous moments, too. “This was no different than the trips to Iraq and Afghanistan,” he said. “You add up all the risks and figure out the tactics that give you the safest option, regardless of whose toes get stepped on or feelings get hurt.”

The government officials and reporters who traveled with presidents to war zones, of course, knew they were doing so, while those left on Air Force One in Ankara last month were not told of the increased threat. Journalists traveling in the back of the plane were instructed while still on the ground to keep their window shades closed during the July 8 flight from Ankara to Britain, where Mr. Trump landed secretly in another military plane. The president was then sneaked back onto Air Force One so that he could disembark in front of cameras as if he had been onboard all along.

The secret switch in Ankara, first reported on Monday by The Washington Post and confirmed by The New York Times and other news outlets, was so remarkable that it sounded like something out of Hollywood. In fact, it defied even the imagination of Andrew W. Marlowe, who wrote the screenplay for the iconic 1997 thriller “Air Force One,” featuring Harrison Ford as a president whose plane is hijacked. Mulling it over on Tuesday, Mr. Marlowe said he was sure the Secret Service was doing what was necessary to keep the president safe. But he added that it did not make Mr. Trump look all that good.

“Now real life isn’t a movie, but given the circumstances, I’m not sure I could ever script a moment like that for a heroic main character,” Mr. Marlowe said. “If the threat were that great, it’s hard to imagine the audience rooting for any character who would trade his own safety by treating the remaining civilians onboard as potential sacrificial lambs, especially without their informed consent.”

The White House did not respond to a request for comment about the calculations that went into the decision or whether extra measures were taken to protect the plane from any threat even without Mr. Trump onboard.

The extraordinary deception underscored the sense of danger felt by Mr. Trump, who was grazed by a would-be assassin’s bullet while campaigning in Butler, Pa., in 2024 and targeted by another armed man at his Florida golf course later that year. During the Biden administration, officials said that Iranian elements were trying to kill Mr. Trump. As recently as Tuesday, the police were investigating a bomb threat at a McDonald’s in Ohio near the site of a planned visit by Mr. Trump later that evening.

The Secret Service and military units charged with the president’s safety typically use decoys to confuse possible attackers, although not involving civilians without their knowledge. When any president travels in a motorcade, there are usually two identical armored limousines or sport utility vehicles with identical Washington, D.C., license plates to make it hard to know which one he is in. When he flies by Marine One, there are often three or four identical green-and-white helicopters flying together.

“If there’s an attack on the motorcade, the secure package splits off and everyone else is on their own, from some WH staff to some military officials, all reporters and members of Congress,” Ari Fleischer, a White House press secretary for Mr. Bush, wrote on social media on Tuesday. “The safety of potus always comes first. We don’t complain. That’s the way it is.”

A president of the United States, or POTUS in government jargon, is at once the most visible and most protected official in the country. The White House over the years has become a virtual fortress, and Mr. Trump plans to expand the security perimeter with a new fence around Lafayette Square across the street from the mansion.

At the same time, a president by tradition always travels with a pool of journalists who record his every public movement and comment. Such constant coverage has been considered vital in the nuclear era when a crisis can confront a president at any moment. Journalists were with John F. Kennedy when he was shot in Dallas on Nov. 22, 1963, and they were with Mr. Bush when terrorists attacked the United States on Sept. 11, 2001.

When presidents have made war zone trips in recent years, the White House typically summoned a select number of news executives to the Situation Room or called journalists to clue them in and swear them to secrecy so at least a few could go along and report about the visits once it was safe. Mr. Bush and Mr. Obama both took reporters with them to Afghanistan and Iraq, as did Mr. Trump in his first term. President Joseph R. Biden Jr. took one news reporter and one news photographer with him on a secret nine-and-a-half-hour train trip into war-torn Ukraine.

When Mr. Clinton traveled to Pakistan, he too switched planes to avoid detection by possible attackers. He had been urged not to go because parts of the country were havens for terrorist groups, but since he was already going to India, he felt compelled to stop in Islamabad for a few hours.

The original security plan called for fooling the accompanying journalists into thinking that Mr. Clinton had boarded the same C-17 military jet that they were on, while he would secretly get onto a separate Air Force version of a Gulfstream known as a C-20. “My vehement protest was you can’t use the media as decoys,” he said. “And they came back with a plan that satisfied me.”

Instead, according to another veteran of that trip who spoke on the condition of anonymity to avoid professional repercussions, they had Mr. Clinton walk around the nose of the C-17 to the other side where three smaller unmarked planes were waiting. The journalists were not able to see which of the three he boarded, but they saw that he had not gotten on the C-17.

Unlike the Trump team in Ankara, the Clinton team informed at least one of the pool journalists in advance, Susan Page of USA Today, who recounted the episode on Tuesday. And the White House then publicly disclosed the details more broadly once Mr. Clinton was safely out of harm’s way. Mr. Trump’s team, by contrast, never disclosed what happened in Ankara until The Post broke the story.

“It’s totally understandable that the White House would want to compartmentalize a security operation like this,” said John F. Kirby, a retired Navy rear admiral who served as a top spokesman for the White House, the State Department and the Pentagon during the Obama and Biden administrations. “I don’t fault them for going to lengths to keep the president safe or in withholding specific threat intelligence.”

“But,” he added, “they also have an obligation for the safety and security of those traveling with the president. And when the risk of that travel is knowable — as it certainly was in this case — they have an obligation to at least provide the broad contours of it so that travelers can make informed decisions.”

Mr. Hagin disagreed. “My only criticism is that it leaked,” he said. “It is very, very hard to move the president covertly, and when you burn one of these tactics it’s unlikely you could get away with it again, which just makes it even harder the next time you need to do it. This wasn’t the first time and it won’t be the last that an operation like this is required, regardless who is president.”

item.title: Warehouse Blaze in Portland, Ore., Is Headache for City Over a Week Later
item.description:
More than a week after a fire tore through a 116-year-old building in Portland, Ore., what remains of the badly damaged warehouse is causing disruptions and frustrating city officials.

The old Centennial Mills building, a former flour mill, sits a half-mile from Portland’s Union Station and abuts railroad tracks. When it went up in flames on Aug. 2, every floor of the eight-story warehouse collapsed. The cause of the blaze remains under investigation.

“A safety perimeter has been set up around the site to keep the public away from the potential collapse zone,” Dan Douthit, a spokesman for the city of Portland, said in an email. He added that the fire had gutted the building.

The city ordered the building’s owner to demolish it by Aug. 14, but the need for specialized engineers and equipment has complicated those efforts. “The building is too dangerous for even our investigators to be near or inside it,” Lauren Johnson, the city’s fire chief, said at a news conference on Monday.

Amtrak train service between Portland and Seattle has been suspended since the fire. The building is near railway tracks and bounded by the Willamette River, and officials are worried that the rumbling of a passing train could shake the building enough to bring it down. A safety zone has been established around the building, and a nearby park has been closed.

But Union Pacific, a freight transportation company, resumed operations on Tuesday in a decision city officials called a “significant risk to health and safety.”

A spokeswoman for Union Pacific, Robynn Tysver, said in an email statement that the transportation company was operating, but with limits. Its trains are running on the track farthest from the structure and traveling under a voluntary speed limit. She said the company was in close contact with the city.

“Union Pacific recognizes the challenges presented by this incident,” Ms. Tysver said in the statement, “but, with no end date on when this long-abandoned property will be demolished, we must consider the disruption the closure of this critical rail corridor has on regional industries, small businesses, ports and consumer goods.”

According to local news reports, Union Pacific did say it would not ship hazardous cargo past the building until Aug. 21.

Portland officials are concerned that the building’s collapse could result in “death or serious injury to those on the train and damage to the surrounding property,” Raymond Lee, the city administrator, said at the Monday news conference.

“We know Portlanders want answers,” he said. “We’re committed to sharing information as it becomes available. But this remains both an active investigation and a dangerous site.”

Amtrak is offering shuttle bus service for some routes, for those who have train tickets, while other routes have been canceled entirely. Customers can rebook or request a full refund at no additional cost, Amtrak said.

The building contained asbestos and possibly other harmful toxins, according to a statement from three investigating agencies, and the city has advised residents on how to more safely clean up ash and debris. The debris from the demolition is another concern the city aims to address.

item.title: Iran Said to Have Known Details of Trump’s Stay at NATO Summit
item.description:
The Iranian threat that prompted President Trump’s secret Air Force One swap last month emerged as he was heading into his last day at the NATO summit in Turkey on July 8.

According to two U.S. officials with knowledge of the threat, U.S. intelligence picked up multiple streams of information. They knew that there was a specific threat of a surface-to-air missile against Air Force One, meaning whichever plane was carrying the president, and that someone in the vicinity of the NATO summit had been spotted with a shoulder-fired missile. And the Iranians knew specifically where Mr. Trump was staying in Ankara, including which floor of the building, the officials said.

The officials spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the intelligence related to the threat.

The information was deemed sufficiently credible to lead Mr. Trump and senior members of his administration to engage in an extraordinary decoy effort to get him out of Turkey. He boarded the older Air Force One in front of the cameras, which he had announced he would be taking “for old time’s sake,” before sneaking off in an airport catering container and taking a military jet out of the country.

Mr. Trump has been the target of Iranian plots in the past. He was grazed by a would-be assassin’s bullet while campaigning in Butler, Pa., in 2024 and targeted by another armed man at his Florida golf course later that year. Those two assassination attempts were unrelated to the Iranian threats.

But a man was convicted in connection with a murder-for-hire plot against Mr. Trump that was uncovered by the Biden administration. That plot was said to be led by Iranians, using a proxy force.

item.title: Trump Administration Bars Medicaid Funding of Transition Treatment for Transgender Youth
item.description:
The Trump administration on Tuesday barred federal Medicaid dollars from being used to provide gender-transition medication and surgery to transgender adolescents.

The treatments are already banned in most Republican-led states, and have been the topic of fraught international debate among health authorities. But most major medical societies in the United States, including the American Academy of Pediatrics, continue to support medical gender transition for young people who experience marked distress over their gender identity.

In a statement announcing the rule, Dr. Mehmet Oz, the administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, a branch of the Health and Human Services Department, said, “Children deserve our protection, not experimental interventions that pose serious risks and convey no proven benefits.”

In a report issued last year, the department concluded that the risks of gender transition treatments — which include drugs that block puberty, hormone therapies and, in rarer cases, surgeries — outweigh any benefits. The report prioritized psychotherapy for minors who experience incongruence between their sex and gender identity.

The new rule, first proposed last year, is the latest in a series of efforts by the administration to block health providers from offering the treatments in states where they are legal. A previous effort was derailed earlier this year, when a federal judge ruled that the administration could not bar hospitals that provide such treatment from receiving funds for other types of care from the major federal health payment programs on the basis of a declaration by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

Transgender rights advocates said the rule would be challenged in court.

“No federal law prohibits this care,” said Josh Rovenger, legal director of GLAD Law, an organization focused on L.G.T.B.Q. civil rights. “Decades of research confirm that established medical care for transgender youth is effective, safe, and essential to their well-being.”

According to a recent analysis by the Congressional Budget Office, the government spent about $100 million on gender transition treatments for minors over the five years from 2019 through 2023. The analysis found that the rate of gender surgery among minors insured by Medicaid was extremely low, at 3.44 per 100,000 among 15- to 17-year-olds.

Under the rule released on Tuesday, health law experts said states could choose to pay for the costs of treatment that federal dollars would no longer cover. The rule also prohibits federal funds from the Children’s Health Insurance Program, or CHIP, from covering transition care for people under the age of 19.

item.title: Darline Graham Advances to the Republican Senate Runoff in South Carolina
item.description:
Senator Darline Graham, the sister of the late Senator Lindsey Graham, advanced on Tuesday to the special Republican primary runoff for Senate in South Carolina, when she will face Representative Ralph Norman, a longtime hard-line conservative lawmaker, according to The Associated Press.

The matchup on Aug. 25 will offer a sharp contrast in experience, though few policy differences. Ms. Graham, who stepped in to complete her brother’s Senate term after he died last month, has offered little in the way of specifics about her positions, other than to back President Trump and the Republican Party line. Mr. Norman is a five-term congressman and vice-chairman of the ultraconservative House Freedom Caucus.

Ms. Graham did not win the special primary outright, despite having Mr. Trump’s endorsement — an outcome, as she said on Tuesday morning, that she expected in the crowded race. Mr. Norman and other more experienced Republicans ran knowing that Ms. Graham, 62, a longtime advocate for people with disabilities, had been largely unknown and untested as a political novice. As of Tuesday, she had been in office for 28 days.

“This is a very emotional night,” Ms. Graham told reporters gathered in Columbia, S.C., on Tuesday night, “because I’m usually standing out here celebrating with Lindsey. I know he’s looking down right now, smiling.”

She rejected criticism that she had effectively inherited the Senate seat, saying that her parents taught her and her brother “that you’re not given anything in life.”

“If you want something, you work for it,” she said, vowing to listen to Republicans on the ground over the next two weeks. “That’s how I’ve tried to live my life.”

She said she had thanked Mr. Trump and was “hopeful” that he would campaign for her, “but we’ll see.” Her family stood behind her in the small recording studio where she made her remarks, without any supporters on hand.

Mr. Norman made the runoff after running neck and neck with Representative Russell Fry, an up-and-coming young lawmaker aligned with Mr. Trump, as results trickled in Tuesday night. Mr. Fry, 41, a two-term congressman from the Myrtle Beach area, did well in South Carolina’s growing northeast. But Mr. Norman attracted strong support around the South Carolina suburbs of Charlotte, N.C., where he is from, and in the upstate region around Greenville, which is rich in Republican voters.

“We have got some socialist Democrats,” Mr. Norman told a gathering of about a hundred people on Tuesday night at a restaurant in Rock Hill, N.C. “This is the party that is intent on taking over this country.”

Mr. Norman said he might not have been the first or second choice of some voters but said he wanted to be their “next choice.” He pledged to run over the next two weeks on a message of faith, family and freedom.

“Let’s win this thing!” he told supporters.

For Mr. Norman, 73, the race revived a political career that had appeared to be drawing to a close after he gave up his House seat and came in third in the Republican primary for governor in June. He was perhaps better prepared than any other South Carolina Republican to run an unexpected Senate race on very short notice after Mr. Graham’s death, having just competed in a statewide contest that had given him strong name recognition.

Mr. Norman did not win Mr. Trump’s endorsement in either the governor’s race or the special Senate race, likely because he backed former Gov. Nikki Haley of South Carolina over Mr. Trump in the 2024 Republican presidential primary. But Mr. Trump’s endorsement in this year’s race for governor did not prove decisive: His first choice, Pamela Evette, the state’s lieutenant governor, made the runoff but then lost. She had faced criticism for relying so heavily on the president’s support that she appeared to campaign on little else.

South Carolina is a solidly red state, but its Republican voters have a long history of rejecting legacy candidates and bucking the party establishment. In Ms. Graham’s case, she has had to contend with her brother’s sometimes difficult relationship with the state’s MAGA voters. They viewed Mr. Graham with some skepticism over his hawkish foreign policy views, his past support for comprehensive immigration reform and his failure to initially back Mr. Trump, though the two men eventually became close.

Ms. Graham has tried to distance herself from some of her brother’s views, saying that she would focus on domestic policy. But she has carefully avoided interviews with reporters and spent much of the past few weeks in Washington voting in the Senate rather than introducing herself to voters.

Mr. Trump held a telephone rally for Ms. Graham ahead of the election on Monday night, saying she stepped up “with tremendous poise and conviction” after her older brother’s death.

“She looks so nice, but she’s actually tough and strong,” he said on the call.

Tiffany Tan contributed reporting from Rock Hill, S.C.

item.title: Ned Lamont Earns Democratic Nod for Third Term as Connecticut Governor
item.description:
Gov. Ned Lamont of Connecticut easily overcame a primary challenge on Tuesday to earn the Democratic nomination for a third term, according to The Associated Press, defeating Josh Elliott, a progressive state lawmaker who ran on a platform of raising taxes on the wealthy.

The A.P. called the race in favor of Mr. Lamont, 72, soon after polls closed at 8 p.m.

Mr. Lamont, who was first elected in 2018, will face Ryan Fazio, 36, a Republican state senator from Greenwich, Conn., in the November general election. Should Mr. Lamont win, highly likely given his durable approval numbers and the state’s reliably blue voters, he will become one of the longest-serving governors in Connecticut history.

Only one Connecticut governor has been elected to a third term in the past 200 years: John G. Rowland, a once rising star in the Republican Party who resigned from office in 2004 because of a corruption scandal, was twice imprisoned and received a pardon from President Trump.

Mr. Elliott, 41, the deputy speaker of the state’s House of Representatives, had sought to cast Mr. Lamont, a J.P. Morgan scion from Greenwich who expanded his wealth through cable television, as a stay-the-course plutocrat who has been hesitant to raise taxes on top earners. (Connecticut has one of the widest wealth gaps in the United States.)

But Mr. Lamont forcibly countered that Mr. Elliott, of Hamden, Conn., was an opportunistic adversary with a spotty attendance record in the legislature and a wish list of ideas not rooted in fiscal reality. Mr. Elliott will still be on the ballot this fall — he was running for re-election to the legislature at the same time as governor.

Mr. Lamont’s tough-minded defense of his record was somewhat of a departure for a governor who had developed a reputation of avoiding flare-ups with political foes on both sides of the aisle, including Mr. Trump.

He presented himself to voters as a governor who has wiped away fiscal deficits, cut taxes for middle-income residents and guided the state through the coronavirus pandemic.

It had been nearly 50 years since a sitting governor of either party had faced a primary challenge. Ella Grasso, a Democrat, was the last in 1978.

A Republican has not won a statewide election in Connecticut in 20 years. The last was M. Jodi Rell, who secured a full term as governor in 2006 after replacing Mr. Rowland. She had previously served as lieutenant governor.

In May, Mr. Fazio advanced from the state Republican Party convention as the nominee, seizing on the withdrawal of Erin Stewart, a rival who was accused of fraud during her time as mayor of New Britain, Conn. Mr. Fazio received 92 percent of delegates’ votes at the convention, more than the 85 percent needed to avoid an automatic primary.

Mr. Lamont has run for statewide office five times in Connecticut, filling the role of the pesky progressive insurgent when he first introduced himself to voters in 2006 as a little-known primary challenger for the U.S. Senate against Joseph I. Lieberman, a Democrat and former vice-presidential nominee who was heavily favored.

Tapping into Democratic opposition to the U.S. war in Iraq, Mr. Lamont pulled off a stunning upset in the primary, only to lose the general election to Mr. Lieberman, who petitioned his way onto the ballot as an independent and later caucused with Democrats.

In 2010, Mr. Lamont lost the Democratic primary for governor to Dannel P. Malloy, who served two terms in office.

Mr. Lamont’s breakthrough came in 2018, when he defeated Bob Stefanowski, a Republican businessman, by just over three percentage points in an open-seat race for governor.

In 2022, Mr. Lamont easily won a second term in a rematch against Mr. Stefanowski.

item.title: Defending ‘Defund,’ Ending Fireworks: El-Sayed Deleted Old Posts and Videos
item.description:
Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan, was a prolific commentator for years, pontificating about the political issues of the day on social media, YouTube and various podcasts.

But if you’re looking for some of his takes from years ago, you won’t find them on YouTube. CNN reported on Tuesday that he had deleted a number of videos and posts where he floated the idea of abandoning fireworks on Independence Day, suggested replacing the Second Amendment with the “right to have health care” and expressed support for the “defund the police” movement.

A review of online archives by The New York Times shows that Dr. El-Sayed has made at least 160 videos from his public YouTube page private, including every post that predated the announcement of his Senate bid in April 2025. He has also deleted numerous posts on X.

He did not wipe away everything.

In one podcast episode from 2023 that was not deleted, he drew a loose link between American football and Manifest Destiny, the trans-Atlantic slave trade and the United States’ history of “destroying Native Americans,” saying that they were “kind of echoed in the ethos” of the sport.

Republicans seized on the newly unearthed content to attack Dr. El-Sayed, who won the Democratic primary last week and is facing former Representative Mike Rogers in a November contest seen as crucial to control of the Senate.

“Defund ICE, defund the police, and now a call to ban fireworks,” Senator Tom Cotton, Republican of Arkansas, wrote on X. “You can’t make this up. The Democratic party has gone off the deep end.”

The videos were made private, which means they are effectively deleted for everyone except Dr. El-Sayed. Auto-generated transcripts, titles and descriptions, however, are available on the Internet Archive and Filmot, which catalogs unlisted videos on YouTube. Because the original videos are no longer available, The Times could not independently verify the accuracy of the transcripts, whose content Dr. El-Sayed’s campaign did not dispute.

Democratic politicians have retreated from some of the more outspokenly liberal positions they took around 2020. Francesca Hong, the front-runner in Wisconsin’s Democratic primary for governor, recently walked back a 2020 social media post calling for Thanksgiving to be canceled, and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a Democrat from New York, on Sunday distanced herself from her calls to “abolish the police” that year.

Dr. El-Sayed’s campaign acknowledged that his YouTube page “was updated to post exclusively campaign content” and suggested that he did not still hold all of the views expressed in the deleted posts.

“Abdul is the former captain of his high school football team, loves Michigan football on Saturdays, and celebrates the Fourth of July with fireworks like the next Michigander,” Roxie Richner, a spokeswoman for Dr. El-Sayed, said in a statement. “Cherry-picked comments from old podcasts don’t reflect his beliefs today.”

Dr. El-Sayed has been unabashed about his progressive views during his campaign, including his belief that Immigration and Customs Enforcement should be abolished. He has pivoted on policing, however.

In one deleted post from June 2020, Dr. El-Sayed called the police “standing armies we deploy against our own people.” In another from the same month, he wrote, “Most major US cities spend WAY TOO MUCH on police departments to police poverty & WAY TOO LITTLE on public schools, health departments, recreation departments, & housing to eliminate poverty.”

He added, “Fixing that is what the #Defund movement is about.”

Last month, he told CNN that he had deleted old social media posts about the “defund” movement because they were taken “out of context” for “clickbait.” And on Tuesday, Dr. El-Sayed’s campaign said that he now believed that funding for law enforcement recruitment, retention and retirement should improve, but that he also supported investing in community programs and other ways to reduce violence.

In one deleted video from April 2023, Dr. El-Sayed opined that the “right to bear arms” was not about allowing people to carry guns, but instead “about being able to sponsor a militia at the state level to protect against tyranny from the federal government.” On Tuesday, Ms. Richner, his campaign spokeswoman, said that Dr. El-Sayed “respects the Second Amendment, and also believes that access to health care is a right.”

In a now-deleted July 2024 video, Dr. El-Sayed suggested that Americans should consider alternatives to fireworks on Independence Day, writing in the video’s description that Detroit experienced “the worst air quality in the entire world” after July 4. “Fireworks just aren’t worth it,” read the title of one section, while another pointed out that they could trigger post-traumatic stress disorder in veterans and pose risks to children and pets.

His campaign pointed to an X post from July 2025 to show how Dr. El-Sayed’s views had evolved.

item.title: 5 Things to Know About the Minnesota Senate Candidate Angie Craig
item.description:
Representative Angie Craig, a four-term Democrat with a bipartisan approach and a plain-spoken style, is one of two leading candidates in the Democratic primary race for Senate in Minnesota on Tuesday.

Here are five things to know about Ms. Craig, 54, who lives in the south suburbs of Minneapolis.

1. She flipped a swing congressional district in 2018. Ms. Craig won her House seat by defeating Representative Jason Lewis, a Republican, by nearly six percentage points in the midterm elections during President Trump’s first term. She narrowly fended off a competitive Republican challenge in her battleground district in 2020 and has since widened her margin of victory in each successive election. Her supporters say her electoral record makes her a safer general-election bet than her Democratic rival for the Senate, Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, a progressive.

2. She supported one of Mr. Trump’s signature immigration measures. Ms. Craig joined nearly 50 other House Democrats in voting last year for the Laken Riley Act, Republican-led legislation directing the authorities to detain and deport unauthorized immigrants charged with nonviolent crimes. After the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown in Minnesota left two U.S. citizens dead, Ms. Craig said she regretted her vote. She wrote in a March opinion piece in The Minnesota Star Tribune that it had “become clear that supporting any bill that gives ICE new authority in this administration was the wrong decision.”

3. She was Minnesota’s first openly gay member of Congress. Ms. Craig married her wife, Cheryl Greene, in California in 2008. At the time, same-sex marriage was not legal in Minnesota. In her youth, she wondered if there was a place for her, she has said. She came out while studying at the University of Memphis. “It was tough,” Ms. Craig said in an interview, recalling that her mother did not know anyone who was openly gay. “My mom and grandmother had raised me. I didn’t want to feel like I had disappointed them.”

4. She had a hardscrabble upbringing. Ms. Craig was raised by a single mother in a trailer park in Arkansas, according to her campaign. To get through college, she had two jobs, opening and closing a McDonald’s and working at a Foot Locker. She went on to work as a newspaper reporter and later as a business executive.

5. She was early in calling for Joseph R. Biden Jr. to leave the 2024 presidential race. Ms. Craig was the first House Democrat from a competitive district to publicly urge Mr. Biden to withdraw after his disastrous debate performance. She has a reputation for splitting with her party, and she casts herself her as an opponent of the Washington status quo. “I’ve done nothing but take on the establishment since I got to Washington,” she said in the interview, pointing to her support for term limits and a ban on stock trading for members of Congress. But some senators have seen her as the choice of Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the Democratic leader, in the Minnesota race. Mr. Schumer’s office has said he has no preference.

item.title: 5 Things to Know About the Minnesota Senate Candidate Peggy Flanagan
item.description:
Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota, an organizer and former school board member running on a progressive, anti-establishment platform, is one of two leading candidates in her state’s Democratic primary race for Senate on Tuesday.

Here are five things to know about Ms. Flanagan, 46, who lives in St. Louis Park, outside Minneapolis.

1. She is endorsed by left-wing leaders. Ms. Flanagan has called for universal health care and an end to unconditional U.S. military aid for Israel, which she has accused of carrying out a genocide in Gaza. She is supported by Senator Bernie Sanders, the Vermont progressive, and Representative Ilhan Omar, a progressive from Minneapolis. She is also backed by the retiring Tina Smith, the Democrat who is vacating the Senate seat that Ms. Flanagan is seeking. Ms. Flanagan said in an interview that she considered herself “an organizer all the time,” adding, “Regardless of what my occupation might be, my vocation is always the same.”

2. She was a mentor to Tim Walz. Ms. Flanagan may serve under Mr. Walz, Minnesota’s governor. But she spent years training liberals considering runs for office in the early 2000s, when she was serving on the Minneapolis school board, and Mr. Walz was among those who came under her tutelage. In 2006, she volunteered on his House campaign. Later he picked Ms. Flanagan, then a state lawmaker, as his running mate in his 2018 campaign for governor. When he returned to Minnesota after joining Vice President Kamala Harris’s ticket in 2024, they had disagreements over shared campaign finances. The governor has stayed neutral in the Senate race, but his wife, Gwen Walz, endorsed Ms. Flanagan’s moderate rival, Representative Angie Craig. “Angie and Gwen have been friends for a really long time,” Ms. Flanagan said in the interview. “ I totally get it. She gave me a heads up.”

3. Her role in the state government has been a target. Ms. Flanagan has faced scrutiny over a major scandal in the state’s safety-net programs. Members of both parties have faulted Mr. Walz and his administration for failing to prevent fraudsters from stealing hundreds of millions of dollars from programs meant to feed low-income children, treat minors with autism and support people at risk of homelessness. Ms. Flanagan has said that Mr. Walz took decisive action to respond to the scandal but that Minnesota residents have a right to be angry.

4. She could become the first Native American woman in the Senate. Ms. Flanagan is a member of the White Earth Band of Ojibwe and has worked to improve relations between the Minnesota government and leaders of the state’s 11 Native nations. She is the highest-ranking Native woman in statewide executive office, according to Advance Native Political Leadership, a group that tracks Indigenous elected officials. Her father was an American Indian land rights activist; her mother, who primarily raised her, was active in the Minnesota Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party, as the state’s Democrats are called.

5. She has called for new Democratic leadership in the Senate. Ms. Flanagan has stood out from Ms. Craig by saying she would not support Senator Chuck Schumer of New York staying on as Democratic leader after the midterms. “People want big, bold change,” Ms. Flanagan said in an interview. “They are sick of nibbling around the edges.”

Ernesto Londoño contributed reporting.

item.title: Rubio, Bessent and Miller Traveled on Decoy Plane From Turkey Without Trump
item.description:
When President Trump took a secret flight out of Turkey last month because of an Iranian threat, some of his top officials remained as passengers on the decoy plane, along with the traveling press who were kept in the dark about the situation.

Mr. Trump boarded Air Force One in Ankara in front of the cameras — but he then hid in a catering container and was taken to another plane on which he left the country. White House officials would not say who accompanied him on the secret flight.

But the original plane was carrying passengers including Secretary of State Marco Rubio, according to two officials who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive information. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was also on that plane, along with Stephen Miller, the president’s top domestic policy adviser, and Steven Cheung, the White House communications director.

Mr. Rubio had been aware of the threat, although it was unclear how many of the others were. At least some of the White House staff traveling on the plane were unaware, the officials said, as were the reporters.

A White House spokesman did not respond to an email seeking comment about the discussions that determined who would be on which plane, and who would travel with Mr. Trump. The email also asked for a full list of who traveled on the older Air Force One.

The Washington Post reported on Monday evening, and The New York Times confirmed, that Mr. Trump took a secret flight out of Turkey amid what was seen as a credible threat from Iranian proxies.
