item.title: 5 Things to Know About the Minnesota Senate Candidate Michele Tafoya
item.description:
Michele Tafoya, who spent years roaming N.F.L. sidelines as a reporter for NBC, ABC and ESPN, is viewed as a heavy favorite in the Republican primary race for Senate in Minnesota on Tuesday.

Here are five things to know about Ms. Tafoya, 61, who lives in Edina, outside Minneapolis.

1. She was one of the country’s best-known sports reporters. Ms. Tafoya’s decades-long, Emmy Award-winning career in broadcasting took her to the Olympics, hundreds of N.F.L. games and five Super Bowls. Her last broadcast was of Super Bowl LVI, in 2022. (The Los Angeles Rams won.) She went straight into politics, serving as a chair of Kendall Qualls’s Republican campaign for governor in 2022.

2. Her campaign has leaned into her connections to football. Ms. Tafoya’s campaign announcement video showed her striding across a snow-covered football field and discussing her career covering the N.F.L. “That job taught me about more than football,” Ms. Tafoya says in the video. “It taught me about how leadership really works. When leaders are prepared and accountable, teams succeed. When they aren’t, people pay the price.” She has spoken regularly about sports during the campaign, often focusing on her opposition to transgender female athletes playing in women’s sports.

3. She supports access to abortion for the first 12 weeks of a pregnancy. Ms. Tafoya has long called herself a “pro-choice” Republican. In an open letter published on her campaign website, she describes enduring five miscarriages and says abortion is the issue she gets asked about most. She writes that she supported the Supreme Court’s 2022 decision to end federal abortion protections and that she believes states should set abortion laws. But she adds, “I do not support an outright ban on abortion, and I believe there should be reasonable access in the first 12 weeks of pregnancy.”

4. She is running without President Trump’s endorsement. Ms. Tafoya may not have the president’s public support, often a powerful weapon in Republican primaries, but Mr. Trump has not endorsed anyone else in the crowded Republican race. Other candidates include the former N.B.A. player Royce White, who was the Republican nominee for Senate in Minnesota in 2024 and styles himself as a MAGA candidate.

5. She has embraced an electability argument. Minnesota has not elected a Republican in a statewide race since 2006, but Ms. Tafoya has argued that her approach could help put the state in play in the national Senate battle. “I’m asking Republican voters to choose me because I’m the proven, electable conservative who will bring some Minnesota common sense to Washington,” she said in a candidate questionnaire published by KAXE, a Minnesota radio station. Still, she has embraced the Trump administration’s handling of immigration after its deadly crackdown in Minnesota in the winter, which polls suggested was unpopular. Ms. Tafoya’s campaign website says the “American people overwhelmingly agree with President Trump that our border should be secure, our laws should be enforced and criminal illegal immigrants should be deported.”

item.title: 5 Things to Know About Michael Alfonso, House Candidate in Wisconsin
item.description:
Michael Alfonso, the 26-year-old son-in-law of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, is the clear favorite for the Republican nomination in Wisconsin’s deeply red Seventh Congressional District.

Here are five things to know about Mr. Alfonso, who has never held public office.

1. He has his father-in-law’s support — and money. Republican candidates in a crowded field for the congressional seat have called out Mr. Alfonso, who is married to Mr. Duffy’s daughter Evita, for leaning on family connections. Mr. Duffy held the office from 2011 to 2019, and more recently he has regularly traveled to the rural, northern Wisconsin district to stump for his son-in-law. Mr. Alfonso’s campaign received $1 million from Mr. Duffy’s old congressional campaign account, as well as donations from lobbyists connected to industries regulated by Mr. Duffy’s Transportation Department. The campaign told The Wall Street Journal that questions about nepotism come from people with “nothing better to do than attack a well-respected member of the administration and his family.”

2. He received Donald Trump’s endorsement. The president, who won the district by at least 20 percentage points in each of the last three presidential elections, in January called Mr. Alfonso a “young STAR” and a “MAGA warrior.” If nothing else, the primary will measure just how strong the president’s grip remains in the district. Mr. Alfonso is a virtual unknown with not much more to show than the word of Mr. Trump, and his primary opponents include a survivor of the Iran hostage crisis. But he appears to be on a path of little resistance to Congress.

3. He would be the youngest member of Congress. At age 26, Mr. Alfonso, if elected, would handily dethrone the current holder of that distinction, Representative Maxwell Frost of Florida, who is 29.

4. He worked for Dan Bongino’s podcast. Mr. Alfonso has a thin track record in politics. According to his campaign, he worked for a year as a producer on a podcast hosted by Dan Bongino, a former deputy director of the F.B.I. in Mr. Trump’s second term. Mr. Alfonso has said he has worked in construction and holds a degree in mathematics from the University of Wisconsin-Madison.

5. Some have questioned his residency in Wisconsin. Mr. Alfonso has said he was born and raised in Wisconsin, and he called Mr. Duffy’s daughter Evita his “best friend from high school.” But Mr. Alfonso was recently registered to vote in Florida, re-registering in Wisconsin with an address for a cabin owned by Mr. Duffy and his wife, according to Wisconsin Public Radio.

item.title: 5 Things to Know About Tom Tiffany, Wisconsin Candidate for Governor
item.description:
Representative Tom Tiffany, whose district covers a large swath of rural northern and central Wisconsin, was expected to easily win his party’s nomination for governor on Tuesday.

Here are five things to know about Mr. Tiffany.

1. He has staked out far-right positions within his party. Mr. Tiffany is a member of the Freedom Caucus, a small but influential group of House members who have pushed the Republican agenda further to the right. He is known for his strong support for gun rights, lowering taxes and opposing taxpayer money for abortions. He was one of 14 House Republicans to vote against a Juneteenth federal holiday, saying at the time that House Democrats had “used their majority to balkanize our country and fuel separatism by creating a race-based ‘Independence Day.’”

2. He is running for governor with the president’s backing. Mr. Tiffany received President Trump’s endorsement and enjoys wide name recognition in Wisconsin as a former member of the State Assembly and the State Senate. First elected in a special election in 2020, Mr. Tiffany easily won re-election in 2022 and 2024. No other major Republican challenged him in the primary for governor.

3. He is betting that socialism will be unpopular with voters. Since he could face a democratic socialist in the general election, he has warned against the dangers of socialism. Francesca Hong, a lawmaker and democratic socialist, was leading in the polls for the Democratic primary on Tuesday. As other challengers on the Democratic side dropped out and Ms. Hong ascended, Mr. Tiffany appealed to voters to make Wisconsin “the firewall that stops socialism from spreading across America” and to “reject big-government socialism.”

4. A general election could be competitive. A Marquette Law School poll last month suggested that a November matchup between leading Democrats and Mr. Tiffany could be narrow. The survey of registered voters showed Mr. Tiffany losing by several points to Mandela Barnes, the former lieutenant governor who has since dropped out of the race. The poll showed Mr. Tiffany beating Ms. Hong by three percentage points.

5. Mr. Tiffany has highlighted his small-town roots in his campaign. He has made the case to voters that with his ties to agriculture and small business, he is well positioned to understand the problems facing Wisconsinites. (One TV ad shows him leading a cow through a barn and saying that the cost of living in Wisconsin is “udderly ridiculous.”) Mr. Tiffany grew up on a dairy farm, attended the University of Wisconsin-River Falls and later owned a river cruise business. He also worked as a dam tender for 29 years.

item.title: 5 Things to Know About Francesca Hong, Wisconsin Candidate for Governor
item.description:
Francesca Hong, a Wisconsin state assemblywoman and democratic socialist, outlasted two more prominent Democrats but still faces several others in the Democratic primary for governor on Tuesday.

Here are five things to know about Ms. Hong, a chef and former small business owner from Madison.

1. She ran as a populist focused on economic issues. Ms. Hong, the child of Korean immigrants, is a single mother and renter who once owned her own ramen restaurant. This year, she was sued over unpaid credit card debt, and has argued such working-class challenges make her well-equipped to understand and improve the lives of Wisconsinites.

2. She canvassed the state to court independents and Republicans. An unapologetic democratic socialist, Ms. Hong has argued that her left-wing beliefs — such as free health care and a pause on data center construction — will resonate across the aisle. She has crisscrossed Wisconsin, including its more conservative swaths, betting that she can convert skeptics in the battleground state.

3. She outlasted more mainstream rivals, including the current lieutenant governor and a past one. Ms. Hong emerged as a front-runner on the strength of her message and campaign organization, but she became the favorite in part because others face-planted. The campaigns of both Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez and former Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes imploded in recent weeks, leaving David Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive who briefly dropped out and then re-entered the race this summer, as her most significant rival still in the contest.

4. She faced criticism for her past left-wing social media posts. For months, Ms. Hong faced attacks for previous tweets calling for abolishing the police. She has distanced herself from those posts. More recently, critics have also unearthed old posts where she took aim at various holidays, suggesting that Thanksgiving is a “colonizer holiday,” that Halloween is “not my thing” and that Valentine’s Day brings out “the worst of humanity.”

5. Establishment Democrats fear her nomination could hand the race to the G.O.P. Ms. Hong has backed away from her old positions and broken with the Democratic Socialists of America on several policies. But many Democrats still worry that her left-wing views could prove to be easy fodder for Republicans in a competitive race in November, potentially vaulting Representative Tom Tiffany, the presumptive G.O.P. nominee, into the governor’s mansion. The party establishment has scrambled to oppose Ms. Hong in the primary’s final days, with Gov. Tony Evers, a Democrat, campaigning for Mr. Crowley.

item.title: In Wisconsin Governor Primary, Polls Have Shown a Progressive Democrat With a Big Lead
item.description:
Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist and state lawmaker in Wisconsin, has been leading the polls in her state’s Democratic primary for governor by wide margins. The only nonpartisan survey since the field settled showed Ms. Hong in the lead by more than 20 percentage points, most likely benefiting from a chaotic race in which the field of candidates competing with her has been in flux for the past month.

Ms. Hong already had a two-percentage-point lead over Mandela Barnes, a former lieutenant governor and state representative, in a Wedgewood poll conducted when the Democratic field was at its largest in early July. Her advantage grew significantly in subsequent polling after David Crowley’s initial departure and the exits of Mr. Barnes and Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez, the race’s more moderate candidates. When the dust settled, Mr. Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, who re-entered the race and was endorsed by Gov. Tony Evers, was Ms. Hong’s chief rival for the nomination.

Polls from “select pollsters” meet certain criteria for reliability and are shown with a diamond.

Polls collected by The New York Times

In all, nine polls were fielded in the three months before the election, but only two have come out since the candidate field settled — and one of those was an internal poll for Mr. Crowley. Even that internal poll showed him well behind Ms. Hong.

Illustrating how support has shifted, a State Navigate poll from late July, when Mr. Barnes was still in the race, showed a lead of 29 percentage points for Ms. Hong. The same firm went back into the field shortly after Mr. Barnes dropped out, and while Ms. Hong’s support stayed steady at 44 percent, neither of her remaining opponents capitalized on the change, with Mr. Crowley and Kelda Roys, a state senator, picking up seven percentage points each, splitting the support that had previously gone to Mr. Barnes.

Primary polling is difficult. In Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, running a progressive campaign, had wide leads in the polling leading up to the race yet ended up winning by a far smaller margin than some had anticipated. But given Ms. Hong’s cushion of more than 20 points, and the fact that neither of the more moderate options has been able to consolidate support, these Wisconsin polls would need to be radically off for this race to be competitive.

item.title: Polling Offers Few Answers in Key Minnesota Races
item.description:
Unpredictable turnout, a large number of undecided voters and a relatively small number of independent polls have created some uncertainty in Tuesday’s Democratic primary for Senate in Minnesota.

While several recent independent polls have had Representative Angie Craig, a moderate, ahead or tied, some partisan surveys released by the campaign of Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, a progressive, have had Ms. Flanagan ahead. In the state’s Republican primary for governor, Mike Lindell, the chief executive of MyPillow and a prominent figure in the election denial movement, has led in six of the seven polls of the race.

Polls collected by The New York Times

Only three independent polls have been conducted since the start of the year in the Democratic Senate primary. All three were conducted by SurveyUSA, and they each point to a tight contest. The most recent of those surveys, fielded a week before Election Day and sponsored by KSTP in Minneapolis, showed Ms. Craig ahead by two percentage points.

The other polls in the race have come from campaigns or partisan groups affiliated with the candidates. Those types of internal polls tend to release results when they are favorable to the candidate or when they advance a specific narrative.

To that end, surveys released by Ms. Flanagan’s campaign have favored her. The latest, from Public Policy Polling and sponsored by the Democratic Lieutenant Governors Association, showed her leading by 14 percentage points.

The most recent poll released by Ms. Craig’s campaign, which was fielded by Global Strategy Group in late May, showed her up by one percentage point — a result more consistent with the independent surveys.

Polls of all types showed a large bloc of undecided voters. The late-July poll for the lieutenant governor’s association found more than 20 percent still undecided, while the most recent SurveyUSA one showed 15 percent in that category.

Polls collected by The New York Times

In the Republican primary for governor, Mr. Lindell has consistently led in polls, including three of the four that were fielded independently.

The exception came in late June, when Lisa Demuth, the speaker of the Minnesota House of Representatives, led in a poll from the Minnesota Private Business Council. That survey was also the only one to show Kendall Qualls, a businessman who was endorsed by the state Republican Party, finishing in the top two.

Mr. Lindell has led in both polls fielded following an endorsement from President Trump in mid-July, but the newest poll, an independent one from SurveyUSA fielded in late July and sponsored by KSTP in Minneapolis, had his lead over Ms. Demuth down to six percentage points. That was a slight decrease from the lead Mr. Lindell had in a SurveyUSA poll from mid-July that was sponsored by three TV stations in Minnesota. With Mr. Lindell’s narrow leads in these polls, the more than 15 percent of voters who were still undecided in each could easily swing the result toward any candidate.

item.title: Areas to Watch in Wisconsin’s Democratic Primary for Governor
item.description:
Until recently, the field of candidates in the Democratic primary for governor of Wisconsin remained in flux. In the end, Francesca Hong, a state representative and democratic socialist, emerged as a front-runner, while David Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, has attempted to consolidate the support of Wisconsin moderates in the wake of recent progressive victories in New York, Michigan and Colorado.

As that familiar matchup of progressive versus moderate plays out, there are a few key areas in Wisconsin that we will be watching after results start arriving shortly after polls close.

Mr. Crowley’s path to victory will almost certainly need to run through Milwaukee. The county, which contains the city of the same name, is the state’s most populous and will account for about 20 percent of the total vote. Mr. Crowley currently serves as the Milwaukee County executive, which could give him a local advantage.

Milwaukee is the state’s most racially diverse county and detailed results here, particularly in the city of Milwaukee, could provide clues to candidate support and enthusiasm among Black and Hispanic voters. Mr. Crowley, who is Black, has gained endorsements from many Black leaders and the Congressional Black Caucus PAC.

This group of Milwaukee suburbs, also known as the “WOW” counties, has been considered a bellwether of the state’s political shifts, and is expected to account for about 9 percent of the total vote. President Trump carried these historically Republican strongholds all three times he was on the ballot, but his margins have slipped since 2016.

The shift to the left escalated earlier this year when Ozaukee flipped to blue in the state’s supreme court election, and how the area votes in this primary could be an indicator of how the Democratic nominee will fare among college-educated, high-income voters — a key group of swing voters in the general election.

Ms. Hong’s base of support is centered in Dane County, which contains the state capital, Madison, and accounts for nearly as much of the vote in Democratic primaries as Milwaukee. Ms. Hong, whose state assembly seat includes several areas in and around Madison, is expected to do well here.

Her lead in polls is particularly strong among young voters, many of whom are concentrated in the areas surrounding the University of Wisconsin-Madison campus. Progressive candidates have historically fared well in Dane; it was Bernie Sanders’s best county in 2016 and 2020.

The three counties surrounding Dane have very different political profiles. Iowa County is the most consistently Democratic of the three and has been an area where progressives have found support in the past. Columbia, by contrast, flipped to Mr. Trump in 2016 after Barack Obama won it by double digits in 2008 and 2012. Green has similarly trended toward Mr. Trump, with Vice President Kamala Harris winning the county by 0.3 percentage points in 2024 after Mr. Obama won it by 17 percentage points in 2012.

Though these counties will not account for a substantial share of the primary vote, they could provide interesting insights into the winning candidate’s strongest coalitions — and where they might have work to do before November.

item.title: Trump-Backed Representative Wins Nomination for Wisconsin Governor

item.title: Klobuchar Wins Democratic Nomination for Minnesota Governor
item.description:
Amy Klobuchar, a powerful four-term senator with broad appeal across Minnesota, won Tuesday’s Democratic primary race for governor, according to The Associated Press.

Ms. Klobuchar, 66, a moderate who faced minimal competition in the contest, jolted Minnesota politics when she signaled interest in the race early this year as a welfare fraud scandal was dogging Gov. Tim Walz’s bid for a third term. Few had expected Ms. Klobuchar to give up her role in the Senate, where she holds the third-highest-ranking position in Democratic leadership.

Mr. Walz ended his campaign in early January, conceding that his sinking popularity stood to hurt Democrats down-ballot. That cleared the way for Ms. Klobuchar to announce a campaign centered on unity in a state that had been gripped by turmoil amid allegations of rampant fraud and President Trump’s immigration crackdown.

Ms. Klobuchar has vowed to be a more diligent steward of taxpayer funds than Mr. Walz, saying she intends to conduct a top-to-bottom audit of state programs and draw on her experience as a chief county prosecutor to root out fraud.

The Trump administration has portrayed Minnesota as an avatar of poor Democratic governance and has sparred with state officials over immigration enforcement, fraud in safety net programs and election integrity.

Ms. Klobuchar has said she intends to leverage the alliances she has studiously built in Washington across the political spectrum — including with members of the Trump administration — to reset the acrimonious relationship between the state and the White House.

“I decided that I wanted to get us to a better place and I could use my skills from many years,” she said in an interview. “I don’t like the status quo.”

As a senator, Ms. Klobuchar has built a reputation as a pragmatist, an indefatigable worker and a formidable campaigner who is popular among moderate conservatives and independents. She was the favorite from the moment she entered the race.

Democratic state legislators and other elected officials enthusiastically lined up behind her and were strikingly candid about their relief that Mr. Walz would not be at the top of the ballot in November.

“She’s tough and gutsy and wildly smart,” Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey said. He added that if she were elected governor, Ms. Klobuchar was poised to become “the most consequential public servant in Minnesota history.”

Kobey Layne, a Democratic Socialist who competed for the state party endorsement for governor during its convention in May, lamented that Ms. Klobuchar was not forced to have more robust debates on contentious issues such as health care reform, U.S. aid to Israel and the future of Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

“I got into this race because people deserve options,” said Ms. Layne, 26, a first-time candidate who favors a single-payer health care system and abolishing the immigration agency. Yet, she conceded her bid against Ms. Klobuchar got little traction, calling it a “David and Goliath story.”

item.title: Areas to Watch in Minnesota’s Primaries
item.description:
In Minnesota, Representative Angie Craig, a moderate, is facing Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, a progressive in the Democratic primary for the U.S. Senate. In the Republican primary for governor, President Trump and the state party are backing different candidates, testing the limits of the president’s political sway. In both cases, the candidates will be fighting for votes in the populous areas in and around Minneapolis and St. Paul, while also trying to build coalitions in the state’s more rural counties.

Polls have showed a relatively tight race in both contests. We will be watching a few key areas as results start coming in shortly after polls close at 9 p.m. Eastern.

The state’s two largest counties, Hennepin and Ramsey, are home to Minneapolis and St. Paul and account for around half of the state’s Democratic votes. The Twin Cities are a hub of progressive support in the state: In 2024, the “uncommitted” movement, a protest vote over President Biden’s support for Israel and the war against Hamas, drew some of its strongest support in the area.

Ms. Flanagan is expected to fare well in these counties, particularly Hennepin, where she was raised and currently resides. She has criticized Ms. Craig’s vote in favor of the Laken Riley Act, which gave ICE broader enforcement powers. That could be a factor in Minneapolis, where two civilians were killed by federal immigration agents in January.

Five other high-income, suburban counties constitute the broader Twin Cities metro area — Anoka to the north, Washington to the east and Carver, Dakota and Scott to the south — and are expected to make up an additional 20 percent of the statewide vote. Ms. Craig represents several of those counties in Congress, and they tend to favor more moderate candidates. In the 2020 presidential primary, Mr. Biden won this grouping of counties by 17 percentage points over Senator Bernie Sanders, while winning Hennepin and Ramsey by just one percentage point.

Rice County, to the south of those key counties, could be an interesting bellwether. A significant portion of it lies in Ms. Craig’s district, including the city of Northfield, home to St. Olaf College and Carleton College, two private liberal arts schools. The high population of college students could make the county more favorable for Ms. Flanagan — in Michigan, college towns were among the strongest areas for Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive who narrowly won the Democratic primary for Senate in Michigan last week.

In the 2020 and 2024 primaries, Mr. Biden fared best in the rest of the state. That could be a promising sign for Ms. Craig.

Ms. Flanagan, who is Ojibwe and a member of the White Earth Nation, could fare better in rural counties with high Native American populations, including Beltrami and Mahnomen.

The Republican primary for governor will test concerns over Mike Lindell’s electability against the power of Mr. Trump’s support. Mr. Lindell, the chief executive of MyPillow and a prominent election denier, scored a coveted endorsement from Mr. Trump, but the chairman of the state’s Republican Party issued a statement criticizing his candidacy.

Hennepin and Ramsey, where Nikki Haley received a large portion of her support in the 2024 presidential primary, are arguably the state’s weakest areas for a Trump-supported candidate. That could translate to more support for Lisa Demuth, the speaker of the state’s House of Representatives, or Kendall Qualls, a businessman and Army veteran who has been endorsed by the state party.

Though it makes up far less of the statewide vote in Republican primaries than it does in Democratic ones, the Twin Cities metro area will still be crucial, with the seven core counties providing around one-third of the primary’s votes.

Both Mr. Lindell and Mr. Qualls have ties to the area: Mr. Lindell grew up in Carver County, where MyPillow is based, while Mr. Qualls ran for Congress in the area in 2020.

Ms. Demuth’s district centers on Stearns County, which is part of the St. Cloud metro area and could be a potential base of support for her.

item.title: Fighter Jets Intercept Aircraft Over Trump’s Patriot Games in Ohio
item.description:
American fighter jets intercepted a civilian aircraft that entered the airspace above a youth sporting event that President Trump was attending in Ohio on Tuesday, launching flares as a warning to the aircraft to leave the no-fly zone.

NORAD, the military command that monitors and patrols U.S. airspace, said that a general aviation aircraft violated temporary flight restrictions — the no-fly zones established around the president and other top officials when they travel — over Geneva, the city in Ohio that was hosting Mr. Trump’s Patriot Games, a youth sporting contest.

The aircraft was safely escorted out of the airspace by American fighter jets, NORAD said in a statement.

It was at least the fourth time that an aircraft has violated the no-fly zone around Mr. Trump just this week. Three aircraft entered the restricted airspace around Mr. Trump’s golf course in Bedminster, New Jersey, on Sunday. The incursions appeared to be accidental, and NORAD gave a pointed reminder afterward that pilots must regularly check for federal notices of closed airspace.

The incident over Ohio on Tuesday appeared to be more significant. The fighter jets dispatched to intercept the aircraft in restricted space deployed flares — countermeasures intended to confuse and defeat heat-seeking missiles — to draw the pilot’s attention and communicate that they had to leave the airspace.

A similar stretch of incidents occurred earlier at Bedminster. On July 19, NORAD F-16s intercepted three aircraft and deployed flares in two of those encounters to ward them out of restricted airspace over Mr. Trump’s golf course.

item.title: Rep. John Larson, a Longtime Lawmaker, Loses a Primary in Connecticut
item.description:
Luke Bronin, the former mayor of Hartford, defeated Representative John Larson in the Democratic primary in Connecticut’s First Congressional District, capitalizing on calls for generational change in the party.

The victory by Mr. Bronin, a former Navy intelligence officer, unseated a 28-year incumbent and followed a series of victories by younger challengers in congressional contests in New York and Denver.

Mr. Bronin, 47, centered his campaign around a call for generational change, arguing that Mr. Larson, 78, was not prepared to confront the challenges posed by the Trump administration’s efforts to aggressively push a conservative agenda through Washington.

“Donald Trump won re-election for a second time, and then we saw a Democratic Party struggle to bring enough energy and clarity to that fight in this moment,” Mr. Bronin said at a debate in Hartford last month. “We would be a stronger Democratic Party if more of our leadership recognized that part of leadership is knowing when it’s time to pass the torch.”

The race marked the first time Mr. Larson, who attracted attention after suffering a complex partial seizure on the House floor last year, faced a serious primary challenge for his seat.

Mr. Larson marshaled much of the party establishment behind his bid, winning endorsements from the state’s entire congressional delegation. Representative Hakeem Jeffries, the New York Democrat and minority leader, held a rally and fund-raiser in the district to benefit Mr. Larson early in the contest.

But he was outraised by Mr. Bronin, who won the state party’s Democratic endorsement and pushed Mr. Larson to the bottom of the ballot in their four-way primary.

Unlike in other races where younger politicians have defeated longtime incumbents, the Connecticut contest did not turn on ideological grounds.

A longtime progressive, Mr. Larson focused on his position as the top Democrat on the House Social Security Subcommittee, saying Connecticut voters would lose power in Congress if they replaced him.

“At a time in this crisis that we’re in, with this unstable president who does not believe or follow the Constitution, with proven leadership that delivers, who’s going be in a position on a major committee, we want to give that up so that we can have someone start at the bottom?” Mr. Larson said in an interview during a campaign stop at a senior center in Hartford last week. “The Connecticut voters are a lot smarter than that.”

But Mr. Bronin questioned how effective Mr. Larson had been in that post, attacking him for failing to advance his signature piece of Social Security legislation for more than a decade, including when Democrats controlled Congress

Mr. Bronin will face Dr. Amy Chai, a physician and mental health advocate, in the general election. Because the district has long supported Democrats, it is widely expected that Mr. Larson will return to Washington for a 15th term.

item.title: Son-in-Law of Sean Duffy Wins G.O.P. House Primary in Northern Wisconsin
item.description:
Michael Alfonso, 26, clinched the Republican nomination for Wisconsin’s Seventh Congressional District on Tuesday in a crowded primary, according to The Associated Press, buoyed by the support of his father-in-law, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, and the endorsement of President Trump.

Mr. Alfonso, who has never held office, is likely to face little resistance in November in his quest to represent the same deeply Republican district in rural northern Wisconsin that Mr. Duffy represented for more than eight years. Mr. Trump won the district by at least 20 percentage points in each of the last three presidential elections.

The president in January called Mr. Alfonso a “young STAR” and a “MAGA warrior.” If elected in November, Mr. Alfonso would become the youngest lawmaker in the House. But some local Republican officials have questioned Mr. Alfonso’s lack of experience and Mr. Duffy’s influence on him.

“I think what they’re doing is wrong morally,” Tanner Hiller, chair of the Iron County Republican Party, told Wisconsin Public Radio in May. “There’s a lot of people that have better credentials, that know this district, that will represent this district better than Michael Alfonso.”

Mr. Duffy, who flipped the congressional seat for Republicans and held it from 2011 to 2019, tested his star power by returning to his old district to campaign for Mr. Alfonso. He emptied $1 million from his old congressional campaign account to support Mr. Alfonso’s candidacy. A ProPublica investigation found that Mr. Alfonso had received donations from lobbyists, business executives and PACs connected to industries that Mr. Duffy’s department regulates.

Mr. Duffy, who got his start in public life in 1997 as a cast member of the MTV reality show “The Real World,” featured Mr. Alfonso this year in a YouTube reality series on his family’s “Great American Road Trip.”

Mr. Alfonso was born in northern Wisconsin, graduated from University of Wisconsin, Madison, with a degree in mathematics and married Mr. Duffy’s daughter Evita Duffy when he was 22, according to his campaign’s website. He said he worked for a year as a producer on a podcast hosted by Dan Bongino, a fervent Trump supporter and a former deputy director of the F.B.I.

Mr. Alfonso has said he was inspired to run for office after the assassination last September of the conservative activist Charlie Kirk, who had galvanized pro-Trump students on college campuses across the country. Turning Point Action, the political organization founded by Mr. Kirk, endorsed Mr. Alfonso for his “unapologetic America First message.”

Other Republican candidates in the race had questioned Mr. Alfonso’s residency in the district. Mr. Alfonso, who was registered to vote in Florida, registered again in Wisconsin shortly before Mr. Trump’s endorsement, according to Wisconsin Public Radio, listing his address as a Wisconsin cabin owned by Mr. Duffy and his wife, Rachel Campos-Duffy, a Fox anchor.

On Tuesday, Mr. Alfonso defeated Kevin Hermening, a former Marine who was one of the Americans held captive when Iranian students seized the U.S. embassy in Tehran in 1979.

Other candidates in the race included an Ashley Furniture executive and a competitive dog musher.

The Republican megadonors Richard and Elizabeth Uihlein backed different candidates in the race. Mr. Uihlein contributed $1 million to Mr. Alfonso’s campaign; Ms. Uihlein contributed $1 million to Jessi Ebben, the Ashley Furniture executive.

item.title: Rebecca Cooke Wins Democratic Primary for Key Wisconsin House Seat
item.description:
Rebecca Cooke, who raised millions of dollars for a campaign that drew support from high-profile Democrats nationwide, won the party’s nomination for Wisconsin’s Third Congressional District, according to The Associated Press.

The district — which went for former President Barack Obama before President Trump won it the last three presidential cycles — is critical to Democrats’ hopes of winning back the House.

The victory sets up Ms. Cooke, a moderate Democrat, to challenge Representative Derrick Van Orden, a hard-right Republican running for his third term who defeated her in 2024 by fewer than three percentage points.

That cycle showed promising signs of electability for Ms. Cooke, a small-business owner and Democratic fund-raiser. Ms. Cooke outperformed former Vice President Kamala Harris by roughly 9,000 votes and Senator Tammy Baldwin, a Democrat, by about 5,000 votes in a rural district that includes a slew of college towns and the city of Eau Claire.

Ms. Cooke did not advance past the primary in her first congressional campaign in 2022. But after her close defeat to Mr. Van Orden two years ago, left-leaning lawmakers from across the political spectrum, including Senators Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Mark Kelly of Arizona, have backed her as the party’s best chance to flip the seat. She is also being supported by the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee.

Ms. Cooke, who grew up on a dairy farm and worked as a waitress, is among a crop of Democratic candidates who have pitched themselves to voters on their working-class backgrounds.

She was one of the top fund-raisers for all House candidates, bringing in more than $8 million from donors across the country. Her challenger in the primary, Emily Berge, the former president of the Eau Claire City Council, raised less than $730,000.

Mr. Van Orden, a retired Navy SEAL, is closely tied to Mr. Trump. He has tried to sell the president’s economic policies to farmers who have been pained by tariffs, rising prices and the war in Iran.

item.title: Matt Little, a Progressive, Wins a Democratic House Primary in Minnesota
item.description:
Matt Little, a former mayor of Lakeville, Minn., and state senator, won the Democratic primary in Minnesota’s Second Congressional District on Tuesday, according to The Associated Press, scoring another victory for the party’s progressive wing in a district long considered to be a battleground area.

The three-way race to replace Representative Angie Craig was seen as test of how liberal candidates can fare in more moderate, Midwestern areas.

Mr. Little, who beat State Representative Kaela Berg and State Senator Matt Klein, centered his candidacy on promises to ban corporate money from politics and support for “Medicare for All.” He was critical of data centers and the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, the pro-Israel lobbying group that has spent tens of millions on midterm races.

His progressive pitch won the coveted endorsement of the Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party, Minnesota’s version of the Democratic Party, which gave him access to the party’s volunteer base, voter list and regional offices.

Ms. Berg, a flight attendant, centered her campaign message on affordability. She was backed by Emily’s List, which raises money to elect women who back abortion rights, and several unions.

On the campaign trail, she leaned into her experience living paycheck to paycheck — like many voters in her district, she said — arguing it would make her the strongest candidate for the party in a general election.

Dr. Klein, a physician who works at the Mayo Clinic, described himself as a moderate in the model of Ms. Craig, who declined to endorse in the race. He focused on appealing to moderate, rural and independent voters in the district, arguing a broad coalition would be necessary to win in November.

The Second Congressional District, just south of the Twin Cities, is the only open House contest in the state. After Ms. Craig won it handily in 2024, it is now considered to favor Democrats.

item.title: A Catering Truck and a Decoy Plane: How Trump’s Great Escape Unfolded
item.description:
President Trump boarded Air Force One on July 8 as a ruse.

On the final day of the NATO summit in Turkey, Mr. Trump walked up the stairway to the plane that was supposed to carry him on the first leg of his journey home. He briefly waved to the cameras and disappeared inside one of the iconic, baby blue 747s that have served as Air Force One for decades. Then he secretly exited the aircraft, hidden inside a catering container.

Mr. Trump was next taken to a military jet for a clandestine flight out of Turkey. The 747, filled with journalists, White House officials, aides and others, took off despite what was deemed a credible threat from Iran against Air Force One.

It was an extraordinary subterfuge, aimed at protecting an American president who has been in Iran’s cross hairs for years.

The latest threat had emerged as Mr. Trump began his final day in Turkey. According to two officials with knowledge of the threat, U.S. intelligence picked up multiple streams of information overnight: that the Iranians knew specifically where Mr. Trump was staying, including which floor, and that someone in the vicinity of the NATO summit had been spotted with a shoulder-fired missile.

U.S. officials immediately began concocting a plan. Gen. Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, was integral to assessing the threat and deciding how to respond. General Caine is no stranger to subterfuge: His last job was Pentagon liaison to the C.I.A., and he helped devise the diversion tactics during Operation Midnight Hammer, when U.S. forces struck Iran’s nuclear sites in June 2025.

Not everyone who rode on the plane without Mr. Trump was in the dark. Secretary of State Marco Rubio knew about the threat and flew on the old plane after helping to plan the operation to spirit the president out of Turkey, according to two U.S. officials. They spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss a sensitive topic.

Other senior officials who traveled on the plane without the president included Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent; Steven Cheung, the White House communications director; and Stephen Miller, Mr. Trump’s deputy chief of staff; as well as several other White House staff, according to a senior U.S. official. It was not clear whether they all knew about the threat.

The elaborate deception — which was first reported by The Washington Post, and which ended without any harm coming to either Air Force One or the military jet carrying Mr. Trump — raised questions about the security trade-offs in protecting the commander in chief.

Whether or not the passengers on the plane that Mr. Trump left behind knew about the threat, they were exposed to risks that the Secret Service deemed too great for the president to face.

On Tuesday evening, in his first public comments about the secret evacuation, Mr. Trump said the decision was not his.

“It’s really just up to Secret Service,” he told reporters after returning from Ohio. “I just follow what they like to do. So I go by Secret Service and the military. They wanted me to go in a different flight, a different plane for safety.”

Here’s how this all came about.

Before leaving the summit, Mr. Trump posted on social media that, for “old time’s sake,” he would fly out on the old Air Force One instead of the luxury 747-8 donated by Qatar that he had flown in on.

He later told reporters that he was sending the donated plane to Europe to “two or three of the big bases” to show it off to the military there.

Mr. Trump then boarded at the front of the older plane in view of cameras and news organizations. Journalists traveling with him, including the New York Times photographer Doug Mills, boarded the rear of the plane and were instructed to keep their window shades down.

What was not known at the time is that Mr. Trump appears to have been quickly taken off that plane via a catering container on the opposite side of the plane. He was then taken to a third plane, which he flew in secret to Britain. That third plane appears to have been a military variant of a Boeing 757 known as a C-32 A, which was parked adjacent to the 747 Air Force One on the tarmac in Turkey.

Video of the departure process shows a catering container on a truck on the other side of the old Air Force One pull away and then drive alongside the C-32 A. Footage reviewed by The New York Times does not have a continuously clear view of the catering container, but it appears that the container is moved by truck from the front of the old Air Force One to the rear of the C-32 A.

A second catering container at the rear of the old Air Force One is also present, but footage shows it being driven away from the old Air Force One.

It does not appear to interact with the C-32 A. The old Air Force One takes off before the C-32 A.

RankUp Aviation

Mr. Trump’s new Air Force One, the Qatari-donated plane, arrived hours before the other two planes at the Mildenhall military base in England. According to livestreams and photographs from that night captured by hobbyist plane watchers and reviewed by The Times, it arrived at 6:26 p.m. local time. The C-32 A arrived at 10:20 p.m., and the old Air Force One arrived nine minutes later, at 10:29 p.m.

There is no recorded flight data for this C-32 A, since its transmitters were not broadcasting its flight path and coordinates. Flight watchers who listened to air traffic control transmissions that night noted on a flight monitoring message board and on social media that the plane used the call sign RCH18 (Reach 18).

Harry Moulton, an aviation photographer who was at Mildenhall and listening to air traffic control transmissions on July 8, told The Times that Air Force One instructed traffic controllers to have the C-32 A land first.

Upon arrival at Mildenhall, Mr. Trump was then secretly moved back to the old Air Force One. According to a U.S. official on Monday, Mr. Trump was taken by vehicle from the plane that he had arrived on to the old Air Force One. He then boarded it through a different entrance and disembarked in view of reporters as he typically would.

He could be seen walking across the tarmac, where he boarded the plane donated by Qatar and flew back to Washington.

Zolan Kanno-Youngs contributed reporting.

item.title: Trump Says Secret Service Ordered Air Force One Swap
item.description:
President Trump said on Tuesday evening that the Secret Service and the military decided he would take a secret flight out of Turkey last month while his staffers and the traveling press flew on a decoy Air Force One.

“It’s only up to Secret Service,” Mr. Trump told reporters after landing in Washington following his trip to Ohio, in his first public comments about the evacuation from Turkey. “I just follow what they like to do. So I go by Secret Service and the military. They wanted me to go in a different flight, a different plane, equal safety but they wanted me to do it. So I do it.”

Mr. Trump’s effort to redirect questions to his protective detail and military advisers came as his administration faced increasing scrutiny over the revelation that Mr. Trump was secretly evacuated out of Turkey on a military jet after the NATO summit last month amid threats against him from Iran.

Despite Mr. Trump and other officials saying publicly last month that he would leave Turkey on one of the older versions of Air Force One rather than a luxury 747-8 donated by Qatar that he had flown in on, his officials had decided instead to sneak him into a military jet via a catering container.

The original plane, however, still carried White House staffers and top officials including Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, along with Stephen Miller, the president’s top domestic policy adviser, and Steven Cheung, the White House communications director.

Mr. Trump on Tuesday night framed the decision as one that was out of his control. “I get a lot of threats,” Mr. Trump said when asked why the Secret Service moved him to a different plane.

“I just have to do what they say,” he added. “They go for safety and I have to do what they say.”

The Secret Service usually works with intelligence officials, the State Department and the military when planning on how to respond to threats against the president overseas, according to former homeland security officials.

Agents in the Secret Service have generally lived by the ethos of bringing the president where he wants to go, even if it means putting their bodies on the line. And Mr. Trump has in the past shown that he has a strong say in the decision-making process over risky movements.

In 2020, while being treated for Covid-19, a masked Mr. Trump took a break from the hospital to drive by well-wishers inside a hermetically sealed, armored Chevy Suburban with at least two Secret Service agents. He also continued to campaign while the pandemic spread, causing some Secret Service agents to privately question whether additional precautions would be put in place to protect the detail.

When asked on Tuesday evening why it was too dangerous for Mr. Trump to fly on Air Force One from Turkey but not too dangerous to evacuate the press, Mr. Trump claimed without providing evidence that the secret plane was actually at “greater risk.”

The plane that the public did not know he was on, rather than the plane carrying his staffers and Air Force One insignia, was the plane they were “more likely to go for,” he said.

item.title: Peggy Flanagan, a Progressive, Wins the Democratic Senate Primary in Minnesota
item.description:
Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan won the Democratic primary race for Senate in Minnesota on Tuesday, according to The Associated Press, defeating a centrist congresswoman in the latest victory for the party’s left wing.

Ms. Flanagan, 46, campaigned as an anti-establishment fighter, calling for universal health care and a higher federal minimum wage. She prevailed over Representative Angie Craig, a moderate Democrat from a swing district, leading by nearly 20 percentage points with more than 95 percent of votes counted.

In her victory speech, Ms. Flanagan signaled that she would focus on the rising cost of living in the general election, and reveled in winning a primary in which she had been heavily outspent by Ms. Craig.

“For months now, I have been telling you that this campaign was about the many versus the money,” she said. “Well, guess what, the many just won.”

Ms. Craig, for her part, said she had called Ms. Flanagan to concede. “Peggy’s story is one of grit, of determination and resolve,” Ms. Craig said in a speech late Tuesday, adding, “To every person that supported me, I ask you tonight to support and elect Peggy Flanagan.”

The Minnesota primary was shaped by a backlash to the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown in the state last winter. Ms. Flanagan criticized Ms. Craig over a vote she made for one of Mr. Trump’s signature immigration policies — a move that the congresswoman said she had come to regret.

Ms. Flanagan, a member of the White Earth Band of Ojibwe, could become the first Native American woman to serve in the Senate if she wins the November general election.

She will face Michele Tafoya, a moderate Republican and a former N.F.L. sideline reporter, in a Democratic-leaning state that has sometimes sent Republicans to Washington in recent decades. Former Vice President Kamala Harris, whose running mate was Gov. Tim Walz of Minnesota, won the state by only four percentage points in the 2024 presidential election.

The winner of the Senate race will succeed Tina Smith, a Democrat, who is retiring.

Ms. Flanagan has said she plans to tie Ms. Tafoya to Mr. Trump, saying her Republican rival would be a “‘Yes Sir, Mr. President’ Senator.” Even before Tuesday, Ms. Tafoya, who was not endorsed by Mr. Trump, had begun to focus on Ms. Flanagan, casting her as a career politician and attacking her over a major fraud scandal in the state government’s social safety net programs.

Ms. Flanagan’s candidacy will offer another general-election test case of the left’s ability to win in competitive terrain. Her victory on Tuesday came a week after Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive former public health official, captured the Democratic nomination for Senate in Michigan, a pivotal swing state.

And it ended a bruising Democratic race in Minnesota. Ms. Craig argued that Ms. Flanagan had unique weaknesses as a general-election candidate, citing the fraud scandal.

Ms. Flanagan criticized Ms. Craig for accepting financial support from corporate and industry groups, including some with undisclosed donors.

Ms. Flanagan was backed by left-wing leaders including Senators Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts. Locally, she was backed by Senator Smith and Representative Ilhan Omar, a progressive from Minneapolis.

Ms. Craig, who raised significantly more money than Ms. Flanagan, drew the support of establishment figures including Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the Democratic House leader, and Representative Nancy Pelosi of California, the former speaker.

Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the leader of Senate Democrats, did not publicly back a candidate.

Governor Walz, who was once mentored by Ms. Flanagan but has had a sometimes tense relationship with her in recent years, also stayed neutral. But his wife, Gwen Walz, endorsed Ms. Craig.

“We’ll all be on the same team come Wednesday morning,” Ms. Flanagan said in an interview on the eve of Primary Day.

Ernesto Londoño contributed reporting.

item.title: Minnesota House Speaker Wins G.O.P. Nomination for Governor
item.description:
Lisa Demuth, the speaker of the Minnesota House, won the Republican primary for governor of Minnesota on Tuesday, according to The Associated Press. She defeated Mike Lindell, who was endorsed by President Trump.

The contest revealed deep fissures in Minnesota’s Republican Party, which has not won a statewide election since 2006.

State party leaders openly despaired last month when Mr. Trump endorsed Mr. Lindell, the MyPillow founder and a prominent election denier who they believed had virtually no chance of defeating the Democratic candidate, Senator Amy Klobuchar.

Ms. Demuth has promised to cut taxes and eliminate fraud in social services programs, a growing problem that she said Democrats who have run the state for the past eight years failed to aggressively address.

Ms. Demuth criticized Mr. Lindell, who has never run for office, as ill suited to take on Ms. Klobuchar in November. She called his proposal to provide legal visas to millions of undocumented immigrants baffling, noting that governors had no direct influence over federal immigration policy.

In the Legislature, Ms. Demuth led efforts to cut spending and to establish stronger tools to investigate fraud. Democrats criticized her for blocking gun control proposals and bills that would make it easier for residents to sue federal immigration agents over abusive practices and bar agents from wearing masks on the job.

item.title: 5 Things to Know About David Crowley, the Democratic Candidate for Wisconsin Governor
item.description:
David Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive and a moderate Democrat, won the Democratic nomination for governor of Wisconsin early Wednesday, upsetting a democratic socialist who had held a significant lead in opinion polls.

Mr. Crowley had dropped out of the race last month, only to jump back in 10 days later and accept an endorsement from Gov. Tony Evers after another leading candidate ended her campaign. Still, Mr. Crowley received far less attention in the race because of the energy that Francesca Hong, the democratic socialist candidate, appeared to be generating from a motivated progressive base.

Here are five things to know about him:

1. He trailed far behind in limited opinion polls of the primary race. Mr. Crowley had been seen as a long-shot candidate going into Tuesday, with Ms. Hong widely seen as the front-runner.

But she also attracted challenging headlines over past comments she had made criticizing holidays including Thanksgiving and Halloween. Prominent progressives including Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York and Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont declined to endorse her. And many Democrats worried that she would not be a competitive general-election candidate in a battleground state.

Mr. Crowley capitalized on Ms. Hong’s struggles, casting himself in the final days of the race as a choice with bipartisan appeal.

His campaign manager, Garren Randolph, said in a statement early Wednesday that Mr. Crowley was now “focused on bringing people together, earning the support of Democrats, Republicans, Independents, and anyone who believes Wisconsin is at its best when we work together and deliver results.”

2. His endorsement from Mr. Evers played a key role. Mr. Crowley found an important late-race champion in the departing Democratic governor, whose decision not to run for a third term set the stage for the contest. Mr. Evers argued that Mr. Crowley would be a strong general-election candidate and that his background leading Wisconsin’s largest county would prepare him for the job of governor.

“He gets stuff done,” Mr. Evers said at one event, adding: “He is an administrator. He is an executive. And he’s got a heart as big as they come.”

3. He would be Wisconsin’s first Black governor. Mr. Crowley has already broken some barriers in Wisconsin. He is the first Black Milwaukee County executive. Now 40, he also became the youngest person to serve in the role when he took the post six years ago.

4. He has said he was evicted three times as a child. Mr. Crowley, who grew up on Milwaukee’s North Side, has leaned into his personal history. Both of his parents struggled with addiction and mental health challenges, according to his campaign. He has said his childhood inspired him to become a community organizer and later a state lawmaker. Even as a child, his family nicknamed him Governor, he has said.

“I wanted to feed my aunt, my grandmother, my uncles, take out the garbage and do the dishes,” he told The Capital Times of Madison. “I wanted to serve my family before I actually sat down and started eating. And so they used to call me ‘Governor.’”

5. He is cautious about proposing tax increases. Mr. Crowley has positioned himself as a moderate on taxes, expressing concern about raising them on the wealthy and calling for a “holistic” review of the tax system.

“We absolutely need to tax the ultrawealthy,” he said at a candidates’ debate last month. “But we need to be smart about how we’re doing things long-term.” And in a post on social media last month about property taxes, he wrote, “The taxes are too damn high.”

item.title: 8 Takeaways From Tuesday’s Primaries
item.description:
An agonizingly close race in the Democratic primary for governor of Wisconsin ended with an upset win for the moderate David Crowley early on Wednesday, the latest turn in a rancorous battle between the party’s ascendant left and its old guard that has defined primary season this year.

Mr. Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive and standard-bearer for moderates in the race, vastly exceeded expectations by defeating State Representative Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist who built a supercharged campaign of energized supporters and overwhelmingly led in most public polls.

Other races were called before midnight. Here are eight takeaways from Tuesday’s long night.

For weeks, polls established Ms. Hong, a democratic socialist, as the clear front-runner. But Mr. Crowley outperformed expectations on Tuesday, narrowly edging his left-wing rival.

Soon after polls closed on Tuesday night, it became clear that, for the second consecutive week in a Democratic primary, a democratic socialist was not winning by as big a margin as predicted. Last week in the Democratic Senate race in Michigan, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed defeated Representative Haley Stevens in a closer-than-expected contest that was not called until the next morning.

But in Wisconsin, the wait was shorter. And the outcome was far different for the progressive movement.

Ms. Hong was the subject of a string of bad headlines in the final days of the campaign, including some over past remarks she made online. Those comments included her derision of Thanksgiving and other holidays, which she walked back.

The negative publicity could have been a bridge too far for some voters, especially if they made their choices in the final days of the campaign. In addition, some of the biggest national names in progressive politics, including Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, sat out the race.

Ms. Hong spent more time campaigning in rural Wisconsin than any other candidate, and it appeared to pay off, given how well she was doing in those parts of the state. Democratic socialists and other progressives have won a string of races on the strength of their ground games and populist left-wing proposals that are resonating with many voters. The old-fashioned takeaway? Showing up in person to make your case makes a difference.

But in Ms. Hong’s race, that wasn’t enough.

In another Midwestern race in neighboring Minnesota, the progressive lieutenant governor, Peggy Flanagan, won the Democratic nomination for Senate, notching a victory for the party’s left wing. Ms. Flanagan’s victory over Representative Angie Craig, who had far more financial resources, was a triumph for what some saw as a more palatable form of progressivism.

Ms. Flanagan ran on a suite of progressive priorities — calling for universal health care, a higher federal minimum wage and an end to unconditional U.S. aid for Israel. She said she would challenge the Democratic establishment in Washington.

But Ms. Flanagan did not describe herself as a democratic socialist, and she captured support from a broader constellation of Democrats and progressives, including Mr. Sanders and Senators Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, Christopher S. Murphy of Connecticut and Tina Smith of Minnesota, whose retirement opened the seat. Ms. Flanagan also did not suffer from a social-media footprint denigrating Thanksgiving. She will face Michele Tafoya, a Republican and former sports broadcaster, in November.

On the Republican side, Senator Darline Graham, a political newcomer and President Trump’s choice to succeed her brother, the late Senator Lindsey Graham, advanced to a runoff alongside Representative Ralph Norman, a hard-line conservative and a leader of the House Freedom Caucus.

Ms. Graham’s triumph over a field of more experienced candidates provided yet another show of the power that Mr. Trump holds over Republicans. The president came around to the idea that Ms. Graham should run for the seat after she was tapped to finish her brother’s term and met with the president in the Oval Office. He made very clear that he admired her poise.

Ms. Graham had been in the Senate 28 days as of Tuesday, exactly one month after Mr. Graham died. In her remarks on election night, she displayed a steady countenance. She talked up Mr. Trump’s domestic agenda while also touting that she passed a bill sanctioning Russia that would have make her hawkish brother proud.

And she let voters in on her grief, saying she has not had a lot of time to process his death.

“I think a lot about what I would say to him, what he would say,” she said. “Right now, I think he would be very proud.”

Mr. Norman, a five-term congressman, had given up his House seat and come in third in the Republican primary for governor in June. His political career appeared to be over.

But running a statewide campaign, even a losing one, gave Mr. Norman the name recognition and organization to jump into the mad dash of a special Senate primary election after Mr. Graham died last month. And that’s what Mr. Norman did, coalescing enough conservative support around South Carolina to advance to the runoff against Ms. Graham.

His advancement also gave Ms. Graham bragging rights as the lone Trump-supported candidate in the race. Although Mr. Norman is seen as a hard-line conservative, his support for Nikki Haley in the 2024 presidential contest may have cost him the president’s affections.

Ms. Graham said on Tuesday that she is “hopeful” that Mr. Trump will campaign for her in the runoff, “but we’ll see.”

Representative John Larson, a 78-year-old Democrat seeking a 15th term in office, lost his primary race in Connecticut’s First Congressional District to Luke Bronin, former mayor of Hartford, in the latest example of restive Democratic voters ousting older lawmakers.

Mr. Bronin, a 47-year-old former Navy intelligence officer, campaigned explicitly on generational change. His victory followed wins by younger challengers in congressional contests in New York and Denver.

Those races pitted younger progressives against older moderates, while the Connecticut race was largely centered on age. Mr. Larson suffered a complex partial seizure on the House floor last year.

Remember Mike Lindell? He lost.

Tim Balk, Julie Bosman, Lisa Lerer and Ernesto Londoño contributed reporting.

item.title: Center-Left Candidate Defeats Democratic Socialist in Wisconsin’s Governor Primary
item.description:
David Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, won the Democratic nomination for governor in Wisconsin, according to The Associated Press. His stunning upset sets up a showdown with Representative Tom Tiffany of Wisconsin, a Republican with close ties to President Trump who easily won his party’s primary.

A surprise surge in the final days of the race helped Mr. Crowley narrowly defeat Francesca Hong, a chef, state lawmaker and democratic socialist who had held a commanding lead in the polls for months. Gov. Tony Evers, a Democrat, endorsed Mr. Crowley, who out-raised Ms. Hong in July with the embrace of the more centrist Democratic establishment, and joined him on the campaign trail, warning Democratic voters that Ms. Hong would likely lose to Mr. Tiffany.

The win was all the more remarkable because Mr. Crowley had dropped out of the race in early July as his support and campaign funds dwindled. He only jumped back in 10 days later to accept Mr. Evers’ endorsement, saying that he and his wife had prayed and arrived at the decision to return. Mr. Evers told Democratic primary voters that Mr. Crowley was the candidate most likely to beat Mr. Tiffany in November.

“We are seeing an incredible shift of momentum,” Mr. Crowley said last week.

During his campaign, Mr. Crowley promised that if elected, he would push to build more housing in Wisconsin, improve the health care system and raise Wisconsin’s minimum wage to $20 an hour by 2030, from the current $7.25.

He faced Ms. Hong; Sara Rodriguez, the state’s lieutenant governor; Mandela Barnes, a former lieutenant governor; Kelda Roys, a state lawmaker; and Joel Brennan, a former state cabinet member.

A Marquette University Law School poll released last month showed Ms. Hong leading the field with 38 percent of the vote, Mr. Barnes with 16 percent and Mr. Crowley with seven percent.

But that field steadily imploded. In the final weeks before the primary, Ms. Rodriguez ended her campaign when she discovered financial mismanagement.

Perhaps the best-known candidate in the race at the time, Mr. Barnes, abruptly suspended his campaign in late July, saying in a message to supporters that it was time to focus on beating Mr. Tiffany.

Mr. Tiffany, 68, grew up on a farm, worked as a dam tender and now represents a conservative-leaning district in western Wisconsin. He has said that his priorities as governor will be to lower taxes, bring transparency to health care and protect farmland in Wisconsin.

Mr. Trump declared in his endorsement of Mr. Tiffany that the congressman has “always been at my side.” As the primary drew near, Mr. Tiffany presented himself as a bulwark against “big-government socialism,” saying that his opponents wanted to empty prisons and abolish the police. He was the only major candidate on the Republican ballot.

“We’re going to paint that clear contrast every single day between the craziness of the left and the common sense that we’re going to bring to Madison,” Mr. Tiffany said at a recent campaign stop.

item.title: After a Typo, Officers Used Excessive Force in an Arrest, a Report Finds
item.description:
Two San Francisco police officers thought they had spotted a stolen car one night in July 2024. After stopping the vehicle, they smashed in a window, dragged out the driver and then tackled, pepper sprayed and handcuffed him. They had the wrong man.

The officers had typed the car’s license plate number incorrectly into their patrol car’s computer system.

A city agency that investigates complaints against the police said on Tuesday that the officers had used “excessive force” during the mistaken arrest of Matthew Ludwig, the driver. They violated multiple policies, the agency said in a report, including spraying him at close range and drawing a firearm without cause.

Despite the case of mistaken identity, prosecutors spent over a year seeking to convict Mr. Ludwig for reckless driving and resisting arrest. Fourteen months after the traffic stop, he was found dead in Kentucky, of an apparent suicide.

“Nothing justifies the amount of violence that S.F.P.D. officers used on Mr. Ludwig, especially when it stemmed from their own mistake,” Brian Cox, who leads the integrity unit of the San Francisco public defender’s office, said in a statement on Tuesday.

While representing Mr. Ludwig against the charges, the defender’s office filed the complaint resulting in the investigation by the city watchdog agency, the San Francisco Department of Police Accountability.

The district attorney’s office, which prosecuted Mr. Ludwig, did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Tuesday. The San Francisco Police Department said it could not comment “due to pending litigation” and referred questions to the city attorney’s office, which said it had not been served a lawsuit on the matter.

It was unclear if the two officers, identified in the complaint as Jonathan Zepeda and Vinesh Govindbhai, had legal representation. Efforts to reach the officers on Tuesday were also unsuccessful.

Based on its findings, the watchdog agency will make a recommendation on disciplining the officers to either the San Francisco Police Department or the San Francisco Police Commission, the latter of which can terminate or decertify officers, Mr. Cox said.

Those recommendations are not made public. The discipline process can be lengthy because officers in California receive significant employment protections.

According to the complaint filed by the public defender’s office, the two officers spotted a Honda Accord late on July 4, 2024, that they believed to be stolen and pursued the driver. Officer Zepeda later said he had observed the car from a distance “running multiple red lights,” according to the complaint.

A few blocks away, Mr. Ludwig stopped behind several cars at a red light. The officers stopped behind him and got out of their car, but did not recheck the license plate, activate their patrol lights, order Mr. Ludwig to pull over or check if his door was unlocked, according to the complaint.

Body-camera footage shows one of the officers, identified in the complaint as Officer Govindbhai, smashing the driver’s-side window with a baton before dragging Mr. Ludwig from the car by the hood of his sweatshirt, pinning him to the ground and bashing his head into the pavement.

Before being forced into handcuffs, Mr. Ludwig can be heard on the video shouting, “I wasn’t doing nothing, bro.” An officer then sprayed him at very close range, directly into his eyes. A short time later, Mr. Ludwig can be heard wheezing and telling the officers repeatedly that he cannot breathe.

“This case shows how easily police can wrongfully target someone,” Mr. Cox said.

According to the complaint, the officers realized only after Mr. Ludwig was handcuffed that they had entered the license plate number incorrectly. But they proceeded to arrest him anyway.

The public defender’s officer said that Mr. Ludwig could not afford the impound fee necessary to recover his car and that the city had sold it at auction. Prosecutors then charged him with reckless driving and resisting arrest.

In September 2025, while charges against him were pending, Mr. Ludwig was found dead at a park in Morehead, Ky., according to the local police. He was 47.

Brandon Coleman, a deputy public defender who represented Mr. Ludwig, said in a statement that as a result of the arrest, his client had “lost virtually everything that he owned,” including his car and a recreational vehicle that he had shared with his girlfriend, which was towed a few days after the encounter.

Before his death, prosecutors had offered Mr. Ludwig’s lawyer the opportunity for him to avoid a criminal conviction if he would take responsibility for his actions.

“But Ludwig hadn’t done anything wrong,” the public defender’s office said.
